The value is in honestly asking ‘how would I break this?'. A small team can threat-model informally — a whiteboard and the STRIDE questions over coffee. As the system grows, it becomes a standard step in designing any significant feature, with diagrams kept up to date. At enterprise scale it's a formal, recurring discipline tied to compliance, with dedicated security review of every major change — because the cost of a missed threat scales with the number of users behind it.

chunks.title: Prompt engineering
chunks.text: Getting reliable, useful output from an LLM by being clear about the task, showing examples, and asking it to reason. Prompt engineering is the craft of writing the instructions, examples, and structure that turn a vague request into a precise, repeatable answer from a language model. An LLM is a next-word predictor that does whatever your text steers it toward. Prompt engineering is shaping that text so the model reliably produces what you actually want — the difference between 'tell me about refunds' (rambling) and 'In 3 bullet points, summarise our refund policy for a customer who is 40 days past purchase' (sharp). The core moves: give clear, specific instructions; set a role and audience ('you are a support agent writing to a frustrated customer'); show a few examples of the input→output you want (few-shot); ask it to reason step by step before answering (chain-of-thought); and pin down the output format ('return JSON with keys summary and nextStep') so the answer is machine-parseable. Because the model has no memory between calls, the prompt *is* the program. Everything it should know — the task, the rules, the data, the format — has to be in the text you send, every time. The same model can be useless or excellent on the identical task depending purely on the prompt — so prompting is the highest-leverage, lowest-cost knob you have. No retraining, no infrastructure: just better instructions, and the output quality jumps. Few-shot and chain-of-thought routinely turn a 'mostly wrong' task into a 'mostly right' one. It's also the controllable, auditable layer. You can version a prompt, review it, and explain *why* the system behaves as it does — far more than you can with the model's opaque weights. Clear instructions: Say exactly what, for whom, how long, and in what format. Specificity beats cleverness. Few-shot examples: Show 2–5 input→output pairs. The model copies the pattern far better than it follows a description of it. Chain-of-thought: Ask it to 'think step by step' before the final answer — dramatically improves reasoning and arithmetic. Structured output: Demand JSON / a fixed schema so the response plugs straight into code instead of needing fragile parsing. Guardrails: Tell it what *not* to do, and to say 'I don't know' rather than invent — the cheapest defence against hallucination. Fine-tuning: Bake the behaviour into the weights. Worth it for high-volume, narrow, stable tasks — but slow and costly to change vs editing a prompt. RAG: When the gap is *knowledge* (the model lacks your facts), retrieval beats clever wording — feed it the documents, don't just ask harder. Tool use / agents: When the task needs real actions or live data, give the model tools instead of trying to coax everything from text alone.

chunks.title: Prompt engineering — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Vague prompts get vague answers, and the model fills gaps by confidently inventing (hallucinating) rather than admitting ignorance. Ask for free-form text and your code chokes parsing it; over-stuff the prompt and the model loses the thread or you blow the token budget and the bill. Worst, prompts are brittle: untrusted user input concatenated into your instructions can override them (prompt injection) — never trust a prompt as a security boundary. Be specific, pin the format, validate the output, and isolate user text from your rules. VERTICAL DEPTH. Local: you hand-type prompts into a chat box and eyeball the results. Production: prompts become versioned source code with a test set of real cases, structured JSON output, output validation, and retries — a regression suite catches when a prompt change quietly breaks an edge case. Enterprise: a shared prompt library with templates, an evaluation harness that scores every prompt change against hundreds of graded examples, A/B tests between prompt versions, and cost/latency budgets per call; prompt-injection defences become mandatory. Planet-scale: prompts are managed assets behind a routing layer that picks model + prompt per request, with continuous offline eval pipelines, automatic prompt optimisation, per-tenant guardrails, and observability on token spend and refusal rates across millions of calls a day.

chunks.title: Vector databases
chunks.text: A database built to store embeddings and find the nearest ones fast — the search engine behind 'find me things that *mean* the same'. A vector database stores high-dimensional embeddings and answers 'which stored vectors are closest to this one?' in milliseconds, using approximate-nearest-neighbour indexes a normal database can't provide. An embedding turns text (or an image) into a long list of numbers — a vector — positioned so similar meanings sit close together. To search by meaning you must answer: *given a query vector, which stored vectors are nearest?* A vector database is built to do exactly that, fast, over millions of vectors. A normal database is great at exact matches and ranges ('name = Rahul', 'price < 500') using B-tree indexes. But 'find the 10 vectors closest to this 1,536-number point' is a completely different question — there's no value to look up, you're measuring distance in high-dimensional space. A B-tree can't help, and checking every vector one by one (brute force) is too slow at scale. So vector databases use Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) indexes — clever structures (HNSW graphs, IVF, product quantization) that find *almost* the closest vectors while skipping the vast majority. You trade a tiny bit of accuracy ('recall') for an enormous speed-up. Semantic search and RAG are only possible if nearest-neighbour search is fast and scalable — and a relational database simply can't do it past a few thousand rows. A purpose-built ANN index is the difference between a 5-millisecond answer and scanning ten million vectors on every keystroke. The alternative — brute-force comparing the query to every stored vector — is exact but O(n) per query; fine for a prototype with 1,000 chunks, hopeless at millions. Vector databases also add the operational glue (filtering, sharding, persistence, updates) you'd otherwise build by hand. Vector store: Holds each embedding plus its metadata (the source text, an id, filters like tenant or date). ANN index: The structure (HNSW, IVF) that makes nearest-neighbour search fast by not checking every vector. Distance metric: How 'closeness' is measured — cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. Must match how the embeddings were trained. Metadata filtering: Combine semantic search with exact filters ('closest vectors, but only this customer's docs'). Recall vs latency knob: Tune how thorough the search is: higher recall = more accurate but slower; the core trade-off. pgvector (Postgres extension): Add vector search to a database you already run. Simplest path; great until vector volume or QPS gets large. FAISS (a library, not a server): Facebook's blazing in-process ANN library. Maximum control, but you own persistence, scaling, and serving yourself. Managed (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus): Dedicated vector databases with scaling and filtering built in — less to operate, more cost and lock-in. Brute-force in memory: Just compare against every vector. Perfectly fine for small, static sets; collapses as data grows.

chunks.title: Vector databases — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: ANN is approximate — push the speed knob too far and the truly best match gets skipped, so your RAG quietly retrieves the wrong chunk and the LLM answers confidently from it. Embeddings drift: re-embed with a new model and old vectors become incomparable (you must re-index everything). High dimensions are memory-hungry, so a million vectors can need many gigabytes of RAM. And mixing metric mismatches (cosine index, Euclidean query) silently returns nonsense. Match the metric, watch recall, and budget memory. VERTICAL DEPTH. Local: a Python list of vectors and a brute-force for loop, or FAISS in memory — perfect for a prototype with thousands of items. Production: pgvector or a single managed index with an HNSW structure, metadata filtering, and a recall/latency target you actually measure. Enterprise: a dedicated vector store sharded across nodes, replicas for read scale, per-tenant isolation and filtering, incremental re-indexing pipelines, and quantization to fit billions of vectors in RAM affordably. Planet-scale: geo-distributed indexes near users, tiered storage (hot vectors in RAM, cold on disk), continuous re-embedding as models improve, and hybrid retrieval (semantic + keyword) fused and re-ranked — serving millions of similarity queries per second.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — AI agents — LLMs that use tools
chunks.title: AI agents — LLMs that use tools
chunks.text: An LLM that doesn't just answer but acts — it plans, calls tools, sees the result, and loops until the goal is met. An AI agent wraps an LLM in a loop where it can call tools, observe what they return, and decide the next step — turning a text generator into something that takes real actions to reach a goal. A plain LLM only produces text. An agent gives that model tools (functions it can call — search the web, query a database, send an email, run code) and runs it in a loop: the model decides which tool to use, your code runs it, the result is fed back, and the model decides what to do next — repeating until the task is done. The key idea is tool-calling: instead of guessing an answer, the model can emit a structured request like search({query: 'refund policy'}); your code executes it and returns the result, which the model reads before continuing. This is how an LLM gets *live* data and the ability to *change* the world, not just describe it. Popular loops formalise this. ReAct alternates Reason ('I need the order total') and Act ('call getOrder(42)'), so the model thinks before each action and adapts based on what it sees. Planning agents draft a multi-step plan up front, then execute and revise it. Agents bridge the gap between 'knows things' and 'gets things done'. A pure LLM can't book a table, reconcile your ledger, or fix a failing test — but an agent with the right tools can attempt the whole multi-step task, adapting as it goes. That's the leap from chatbot to *coworker*. Versus hard-coding every step yourself: an agent handles tasks whose steps you can't fully predict in advance ('investigate why this order is stuck'), choosing tools dynamically. The price is unpredictability — which is exactly why the guardrails matter. The model (reasoner): The LLM that decides what to do next, given the goal and everything observed so far. Tools: Functions the model may call — each with a name, a description, and a typed schema for its arguments. The loop (executor): Your code: ask the model, run the tool it chose, feed the result back, repeat until done or capped. Memory / scratchpad: The running record of steps, observations, and partial results the model reads each turn. Stop conditions: Limits — max steps, budget, a 'done' signal — so the loop can't run forever or burn unlimited money. Single tool-call (no loop): Let the model call one function and answer. Far more predictable and cheaper; enough for most 'fetch then respond' tasks. A fixed workflow / pipeline: Hard-code the steps and call the LLM only where judgement is needed. Boring, reliable, debuggable — prefer it when steps are known. RAG: If the task is really 'answer from my knowledge', retrieval is simpler and safer than a free-roaming agent.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — AI agents — LLMs that use tools
chunks.title: AI agents — LLMs that use tools — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Agents can loop forever, rack up huge bills, or take a confidently wrong action — because the model's plan can be subtly wrong and each step compounds the last. A tool that *changes the world* (sends money, deletes rows) executed on a hallucinated argument is a real-world incident, not a typo. Prompt injection is acute here: malicious text in a web page or document the agent reads can hijack it into misusing its tools. Cap steps and budget, validate every tool call, sandbox dangerous actions, and keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible. VERTICAL DEPTH. Local: a single agent, a couple of read-only tools, a step cap, run by hand — you watch every step in the console. Production: validated tool schemas, sandboxed execution, per-task budgets and timeouts, full tracing of every step, and human approval gates on irreversible actions. Enterprise: a fleet of specialised agents behind a queue, each with least-privilege credentials and audit logging, a tool registry with access control, evaluation suites that grade agent runs, and circuit-breakers that disable a misbehaving agent. Planet-scale: thousands of concurrent agent runs orchestrated across workers, cost and safety monitored in real time, multi-agent systems where a planner delegates to sub-agents, with global rate limits, regional isolation, and continuous red-teaming against injection at the edge.

chunks.title: RAG vs fine-tuning
chunks.text: Two ways to give a model your knowledge — look it up at answer time (RAG), or bake it into the weights (fine-tuning). When to use which. RAG feeds the model relevant facts at query time and keeps knowledge external and fresh; fine-tuning trains those patterns into the model's weights and changes how it behaves — they solve different problems and are often combined. A base LLM only knows what it saw in training — not your private docs, and nothing newer than its cutoff. There are two ways to fix that gap. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) retrieves the most relevant pieces of *your* data at answer time and pastes them into the prompt, so the model answers from facts it can see right now. Fine-tuning instead continues training the model on your examples, adjusting its weights so the knowledge or behaviour is *baked in* — no documents needed at query time, the model just 'knows' it. The mental split: **RAG changes what the model can *see*; fine-tuning changes what the model *is*.** The decisive question is *what kind of gap you're closing*. Missing facts (policies, product data, anything that changes)? That's a retrieval problem → RAG. Wrong behaviour, style, or format (always reply in our brand voice, always emit this exact JSON, handle this niche task)? That's a weights problem → fine-tuning. Picking the wrong tool wastes money and produces a worse product: fine-tuning to teach facts gives you a model that's expensive, slow to update, and *still* hallucinates when facts change; bolting RAG onto a styling problem leaves the tone wrong no matter how good the retrieval. Matching the technique to the gap is the whole game. RAG's superpower is freshness and traceability — the answer is grounded in a document you can show. Fine-tuning's superpower is that the behaviour is intrinsic and the prompt stays small. They're complementary, not rivals. Freshness: RAG: update a document, the next answer reflects it instantly. Fine-tuning: stale until you retrain. What it's good at: RAG: facts, private/up-to-date knowledge, citations. Fine-tuning: style, format, tone, narrow skills. Cost & speed: RAG: cheap, fast to set up and change. Fine-tuning: costly compute, slow iteration, harder to undo. Explainability: RAG can cite the source chunk it used. Fine-tuning is a black box — you can't point to *why*. Inference cost: RAG adds retrieved text to every prompt (more tokens). Fine-tuning needs no extra context, so prompts stay short. Prompt engineering only: No data pipeline, no training — just better instructions and examples. Always try this first; it's often enough. Long context (stuff everything in): Paste all docs into a big-context model. Dead simple, but costly per call and dilutes relevance as docs grow. RAG + fine-tuning together: Fine-tune the behaviour, retrieve the facts — the common setup for serious assistants.

chunks.title: RAG vs fine-tuning — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The classic failure is using fine-tuning as a knowledge store: you train in last quarter's facts, they go stale, retraining is slow and pricey, and the model *still* confidently hallucinates on anything it didn't memorise. The opposite failure is expecting RAG to fix *behaviour* — no amount of retrieved text makes a model adopt your tone or output format if it won't follow the instruction. And reaching for either before trying prompt engineering burns time and money on a problem a better prompt would have solved. Diagnose the gap (facts vs behaviour) before picking the tool. VERTICAL DEPTH. Local: prompt engineering on a base model — no retrieval, no training; you discover where it falls short. Production: add RAG over a small vector store for facts, and fine-tune only if a stubborn behaviour/format problem survives good prompting; measure both. Enterprise: a retrieval platform with evaluated chunking and re-ranking, plus a fine-tuning pipeline with versioned datasets and eval gates; teams choose per use-case via a shared decision framework. Planet-scale: continuously refreshed retrieval indexes feeding many products, periodic fine-tunes (and adapters/LoRA) layered per domain, automated evals deciding when a retrain is justified, and routing that sends each request to the right model+strategy — all under tight cost and latency budgets across millions of calls.

chunks.title: The OWASP Top 10
chunks.text: The industry's canonical shortlist of the most common, most damaging web vulnerabilities — the checklist every web app should be measured against. The OWASP Top 10 is a regularly-updated, community-built list of the ten broadest categories of web-application security risk, used as a shared baseline for what to defend against and test for. OWASP (the Open Worldwide Application Security Project) is a non-profit that publishes free security knowledge. Its most famous output is the Top 10: a ranked list of the ten *categories* of web vulnerability that cause the most real-world damage, refreshed every few years from data across thousands of applications. It's deliberately a list of categories, not individual bugs — broad themes like 'broken access control' or 'injection' — so it stays a stable mental checklist rather than a list of specific exploits that go out of date. If you're secure against all ten categories, you've covered the failures that actually hurt most teams. The headline entries you'll hear most: Broken Access Control (users reaching data or actions they shouldn't — consistently #1), Injection (SQLi/XSS-style 'input becomes code'), Cryptographic Failures (secrets sent or stored unprotected), Security Misconfiguration (defaults left on, debug exposed), and Vulnerable Components (out-of-date libraries with known holes). Without a shared baseline, every team guesses at what 'secure enough' means and misses the same well-known failures. The Top 10 gives auditors, developers, and clients a *common language* — 'we test against the OWASP Top 10' is an industry-understood claim — and concentrates effort on the risks that statistically cause the most breaches. It's also evidence-driven: the rankings come from real incident data, so you're prioritising by actual impact, not folklore. Broken access control sits at #1 because that's what keeps getting exploited. Broken Access Control: Users do or see things they shouldn't — the perennial #1. The fix lives in checks on the *server*, never the UI. Injection: Untrusted input is executed as code — SQLi, XSS, command injection. Cured by separating data from commands. Cryptographic Failures: Sensitive data exposed: no HTTPS, plaintext passwords, weak or home-rolled crypto. Security Misconfiguration: Insecure defaults, verbose error pages, open admin endpoints, permissions too wide. Vulnerable & Outdated Components: A dependency with a known CVE — you inherit every hole in code you didn't write. OWASP ASVS: A far more detailed, level-based verification standard. Use it when the Top 10 is too coarse and you need exhaustive requirements. CWE / CVE catalogues: Granular databases of specific weakness types and known vulnerabilities — reference material, not a prioritised shortlist. Threat modelling: Reasons about *your* specific system's threats rather than generic categories — complementary, not a replacement.

chunks.title: The OWASP Top 10 — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Treating the Top 10 as a *complete* security program is the trap — it's a floor, not a ceiling: it covers common categories, not your app's unique business-logic flaws (a discount that can go negative, an order that can be claimed twice). It's also category-level, so a green checkmark hides specifics; 'we handle injection' means nothing if one query still concatenates strings. And it shifts over time — citing an old edition can mean defending against yesterday's priorities. Use it as the baseline, then go deeper with threat modelling and the ASVS. VERTICAL DEPTH. Local: read the list once and self-review your app against it before sharing it — catch the obvious own-goals. Production: the Top 10 becomes mandatory pre-launch checks — dependency scanning and basic SAST in CI, access-control tests, HTTPS everywhere, no debug endpoints exposed. Enterprise: it's woven into the SDLC — secure-coding standards mapped to each category, automated SAST/DAST/dependency gates blocking risky merges, periodic third-party pen-tests scoped to the Top 10 and ASVS, and security training built around it. Planet-scale: a dedicated AppSec org runs continuous scanning across thousands of services, bug-bounty programs, automated CVE remediation pipelines, runtime protections (WAF, RASP) tuned to these categories, and metrics tracking time-to-patch — the Top 10 is the shared vocabulary, but defence is continuous and org-wide.

chunks.title: Cryptography basics
chunks.text: The three building blocks — encryption, hashing, and signatures — and exactly what each one does and doesn't guarantee. Encryption keeps data secret, hashing fingerprints it irreversibly, and digital signatures prove who sent it and that it wasn't changed — three different tools for three different guarantees. Cryptography boils down to three tools, and the #1 beginner mistake is confusing them. Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the right key can unscramble it — it's reversible and provides confidentiality (secrecy). Hashing turns data into a fixed-size fingerprint that *can't* be reversed — it provides integrity (detecting change) and is how passwords are stored. Digital signatures prove a message came from a specific sender and wasn't altered — providing authenticity and non-repudiation. Encryption itself comes in two flavours. Symmetric encryption uses *one shared key* to both lock and unlock — fast, but both sides must already share the secret. Asymmetric (public-key) encryption uses a *pair*: a public key anyone can have, and a private key kept secret; what one locks, only the other unlocks — which lets strangers exchange secrets without a pre-shared key. The crucial rule of thumb: hashing is not encryption (you can never get the original back from a hash), and encryption is not a signature (hiding data doesn't prove who sent it). Each guarantee needs its own tool. Almost every security guarantee on the internet is one of these three primitives: HTTPS (encryption + signatures), stored passwords (hashing), software updates and JWTs (signatures), API secrets (encryption). Knowing *which guarantee each gives* is what lets you pick the right one instead of, say, 'encrypting' a password (reversible — wrong) or 'hashing' data you need to read back (impossible — wrong). The alternative — trusting the network or storing secrets in plaintext — fails catastrophically the moment anyone untrusted sees the data. These tools make eavesdropping, tampering, and impersonation computationally infeasible. Symmetric encryption: One shared key locks and unlocks (AES). Fast — used for the bulk of real data — but you must share the key safely. Asymmetric encryption: A public/private key pair (RSA, elliptic-curve). Lets strangers share secrets; slower, so used to set up symmetric keys. Hashing: One-way fingerprint (SHA-256). Same input → same hash; can't be reversed. For integrity checks and (salted) passwords. Digital signature: Sign with your private key; anyone verifies with your public key. Proves authorship + that nothing changed. Salt: Random data mixed into each password hash so identical passwords get different hashes — defeats precomputed-table attacks. Encoding (Base64, hex): NOT security — it's reversible by anyone with no key. A common dangerous mix-up: encoding hides nothing. Hashing vs encryption for storage: Hash what you only need to *verify* (passwords); encrypt what you need to *read back* (a stored API token). Symmetric vs asymmetric: Symmetric is fast for bulk data; asymmetric solves key exchange and signing. Real systems use both together.

chunks.title: Cryptography basics — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The dangerous failures are conceptual: encrypting passwords instead of hashing them (a stolen key reverses them all), hashing with a fast unsalted algorithm like raw SHA-256 (rainbow-table-cracked in seconds), confusing encoding with encryption (Base64 protects nothing), or rolling your own crypto (subtle flaws break it completely — even experts use audited libraries). And all of it collapses if the keys leak: cryptography just moves the secret into the key, so key management *is* the security. Pick the primitive that matches the guarantee, use vetted libraries, and protect the keys. VERTICAL DEPTH. Local: call a trusted library — bcrypt for passwords, the platform's TLS, a standard sign/verify function — and never touch the math yourself. Production: enforce HTTPS everywhere, salt+slow-hash all passwords, sign tokens and webhooks, and store secrets in a vault rather than code or env files in the repo. Enterprise: a key-management system (KMS/HSM) with strict access control, automated key and certificate rotation, encryption-at-rest for databases and backups, and mTLS between internal services. Planet-scale: dedicated hardware security modules, regional key hierarchies and envelope encryption (data keys wrapped by master keys), automated certificate issuance for thousands of services, crypto-agility to swap algorithms ahead of threats, and a roadmap toward post-quantum algorithms — all audited continuously.

chunks.title: OAuth & OpenID Connect
chunks.text: 'Sign in with Google' explained — how an app gets permission to act on your behalf, and how it learns who you are, without ever seeing your password. OAuth 2.0 lets an app get limited permission (a token) to access your data on another service without your password; OpenID Connect adds a verified answer to 'who is this user?' — that combination is what powers social login. Two different questions hide behind 'Sign in with Google'. Authorization = 'what is this app *allowed to do*?' (read your contacts, post on your behalf). Authentication = 'who *is* this user?'. OAuth 2.0 solves the first; OpenID Connect (OIDC), a thin layer on top of OAuth, solves the second. Mixing them up is the classic confusion. The magic of OAuth is delegated access without sharing your password. Instead of giving an app your Google password (terrifying — it could do anything, forever), Google hands the app a scoped, expiring access token: 'this app may read your calendar, for one hour, and nothing else'. You can revoke it anytime, and the app never sees your credentials. OIDC adds an ID token (a signed JWT) that *proves who you are* — your verified user id, name, email — so the app can log you in. So 'Sign in with Google' is really: OIDC to identify you + OAuth tokens to (optionally) access your Google data. Before OAuth, apps that wanted your data asked for your actual password to the other service — a disaster: full access, forever, no scoping, no revocation, and your password copied everywhere. OAuth replaces that with *scoped, expiring, revocable* tokens issued by the provider, so a breached app leaks a limited token, not your master credentials. OIDC then standardises identity so every app doesn't reinvent login — users get one trusted account, apps offload password storage and 2FA to a specialist provider (less to get wrong), and single sign-on across many apps becomes possible. Resource owner: You — the user who owns the data and grants permission. Client: The app asking for access (the website with the 'Sign in with Google' button). Authorization server: The provider that authenticates you and issues tokens (Google, Auth0, your identity provider). Access token: Short-lived OAuth credential the client uses to call APIs on your behalf, limited to granted scopes. ID token (OIDC): A signed JWT that *proves who you are* — the piece that actually logs you in. Username + password (own auth): You store and verify credentials yourself. Full control, but you carry all the risk — hashing, resets, 2FA, breaches. SAML: An older XML-based SSO standard, still common in enterprises; OIDC is the modern, JSON/JWT successor for new apps. API keys / personal tokens: Simple long-lived secrets for machine-to-machine access — no user, no consent flow, but easy to leak and rarely scoped.

chunks.title: OAuth & OpenID Connect — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: OAuth is powerful but easy to implement *insecurely*, and the failures are severe. Using the old implicit flow (tokens in the URL) leaks them via history and referrers — use Authorization Code + PKCE. Skipping the state parameter opens you to CSRF on the callback; not validating the ID token's signature, issuer, and audience lets an attacker forge identity; over-broad scopes hand apps far more than they need; and leaked refresh tokens are long-lived skeleton keys. The deepest trap is the conceptual one — using an *access token* (authorization) as proof of *identity* (authentication), which is what OIDC's ID token exists to fix. Follow the spec's recommended flow, validate every token, and request the least scope. VERTICAL DEPTH. Local: one 'Sign in with Google' button via a library, redirect URIs pointed at localhost — you just want login working. Production: Authorization Code + PKCE, server-side token exchange, validated ID tokens, secure refresh-token storage, least-privilege scopes, and the state check — login that's actually safe. Enterprise: a central identity provider (Okta, Auth0, Entra) brokering SSO across dozens of internal apps, role/scope governance, short token lifetimes with rotation, and audit logs of every grant. Planet-scale: a federated identity platform issuing tokens for thousands of services and millions of users, multi-region authorization servers, fine-grained scopes and consent, token introspection/revocation at the edge, continuous monitoring for token abuse, and step-up auth (re-prompt for sensitive actions) woven throughout.

chunks.title: API gateways
chunks.text: The single front door every request walks through before it reaches any of your services. An API gateway is one entry point in front of your backend that routes each request to the right service and handles the cross-cutting jobs — auth, rate-limiting, TLS — in one place so every service doesn't reinvent them. As soon as a system grows past one backend, clients face a problem: *which* server do I call, and how do I prove who I am to each one? An API gateway answers that by being the single public address clients talk to. It receives every request, figures out where it belongs, and forwards it on — clients never need to know how many services exist behind it or where they live. Beyond routing, a gateway is the natural home for the work that *every* request needs but no single service should own: terminating TLS (decrypting HTTPS), checking auth tokens, enforcing rate limits, adding a request-id for tracing, and logging. Doing these once at the edge means each service behind the gateway can stay focused on its actual job. A gateway can also aggregate: a mobile screen that needs the menu, the cart, and the user's points might make one call to the gateway, which fans out to three services and stitches the answers together — so the phone makes one round-trip instead of three over a slow network. Without a gateway, every service has to implement auth, TLS, rate-limiting, and logging itself — and they'll do it slightly differently, leaving gaps an attacker can find. Centralising those concerns makes them consistent and auditable, and lets you change a policy (a new rate limit, a new auth scheme) in one place. It also decouples clients from your internal architecture. You can split one service into three, move them between machines, or rename internal paths — and as long as the gateway's public routes stay stable, no client ever notices. That freedom to reshape the backend is worth a lot. Routing: Maps an incoming path (/api/orders) to the service that owns it, hiding the backend's internal shape from clients. Auth & TLS termination: Decrypts HTTPS and verifies the caller's token once, at the edge, before any service sees the request. Rate-limiting & throttling: Caps how fast any one client can call, protecting everything behind it from floods. Aggregation: Calls several services for one client request and combines the results into a single response. Cross-cutting plumbing: Adds request-ids, logs, collects metrics, and can cache hot responses — uniformly, for all traffic. Direct-to-service (no gateway): Simplest for one or two services; clients call them directly. Breaks down fast as services multiply and each must own its own edge concerns. Reverse proxy (nginx/Envoy): A lighter front door that routes and terminates TLS but does less app-aware work; often *is* the gateway's engine underneath. Service mesh: Pushes routing/auth/retries *between* internal services (sidecars), complementing rather than replacing the public gateway. BFF (backend-for-frontend): A per-client gateway tuned to one app's screens; great for aggregation, but one more service to run per client type.

chunks.title: API gateways — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Make the gateway a single point of failure with no redundancy and the day it falls, *everything* falls — every service is unreachable even though they're all healthy. Forget timeouts on aggregation and one slow downstream service hangs every request that touches it. Put too much business logic in the gateway and it becomes a tangled bottleneck every team must edit and fear. The gateway should be thin, replicated, and ruthless about cross-cutting concerns only. Local: no gateway — you call your one backend directly on localhost. Production: a single reverse proxy (nginx/Caddy) in front terminating TLS, rate-limiting, and routing to your app — already a real gateway. Enterprise: a clustered gateway (Kong/Apigee/Envoy) fronting dozens of services, with central auth, per-route policies, and a service mesh handling internal traffic. Planet-scale: gateways replicated in every region behind global anycast, so a request enters at the nearest edge, gets authed and rate-limited locally, and only the necessary calls travel further — the front door is everywhere at once.

chunks.title: Caching strategies
chunks.text: Not just *whether* to cache, but *how* reads and writes flow through the cache — and how each one can lie to you. Caching strategies are the named patterns — cache-aside, write-through, write-back — for deciding when data enters and leaves the cache, what to evict when it's full, and how to invalidate copies that have gone stale. Once you've decided to cache (see caching), the real engineering question is *the flow*: when does data get into the cache, and when does a write update or remove it? Pick the wrong pattern and you'll serve stale prices, lose writes on a crash, or stampede your database the instant a popular key expires. There are three classic read/write patterns. Cache-aside (lazy): the app checks the cache; on a miss it reads the database, then stores the result for next time. Write-through: every write goes to the cache *and* the database together, so the cache is always fresh. Write-back (write-behind): writes go to the cache immediately and are flushed to the database later in a batch — fast, but risky if the cache dies before the flush. Two cross-cutting concerns sit on top of any pattern. Eviction decides what to throw out when the cache fills up (commonly LRU — least recently used). Invalidation decides when a cached copy is *wrong* and must go — the genuinely hard part, because nothing about the cached value itself tells you the source data changed underneath it. Each pattern is a deliberate trade between freshness, write speed, and durability. Cache-aside is the default because it's simple and the cache never holds data the database doesn't — but it accepts a slow first read and a brief stale window. Write-through buys always-fresh reads at the cost of slower writes. Write-back buys blistering writes at the cost of possibly losing them. Knowing which you've chosen is knowing exactly which failure you've accepted. Eviction and invalidation matter because a cache is *finite* and *derivative*: it will always be too small to hold everything, and its contents are always a possibly-outdated copy of something else. Choosing the eviction policy decides what stays fast; choosing the invalidation rule decides whether ‘fast' is also ‘correct'. Cache-aside: App reads cache, falls back to DB on a miss, then populates the cache. The most common, most flexible pattern. Write-through: Writes hit cache and DB together; reads are always fresh, writes pay a small latency tax. Write-back: Writes hit cache now, DB later in batches. Fastest writes, but unflushed data is lost if the cache crashes. Eviction (LRU/LFU/TTL): What to drop when full: least-recently-used, least-frequently-used, or simply ‘expire after N seconds'. Invalidation: Removing or refreshing a key when the underlying data changes — by TTL, by explicit delete-on-write, or by event. Cache-aside: Default. Simple, resilient (a cache outage just means slower reads), but accepts cold-miss latency and a stale window. Write-through: Reads always fresh; every write is a touch slower. Good when reads vastly outnumber writes and staleness is intolerable. Write-back: Fastest writes by far; risks losing recent writes on a cache crash. Reserve for tolerant, high-write workloads. Read-through (managed): The cache library itself loads from the DB on a miss, hiding the fallback from your app — tidy, but ties you to that library.

chunks.title: Caching strategies — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Update the cache on write instead of deleting it, and a slow writer can stamp an old value over a newer one — a stale read that never self-heals. Choose write-back without understanding it and a cache crash silently loses the last minute of orders. Give every key the same TTL and they all expire together, stampeding the database at the same instant. Cache something user-specific under a shared key and one customer sees another's data. The pattern you didn't think about is the bug you'll ship. Local: a plain in-memory map (cache-aside) inside your one process — gone on restart, and that's fine. Production: a shared Redis with cache-aside and sensible TTLs, plus delete-on-write invalidation so an admin price change is reflected on the next read. Enterprise: tiered caching — per-process L1 in front of a shared Redis L2 — with stampede protection, jittered TTLs, and event-driven invalidation fired from a message queue. Planet-scale: regional cache clusters plus a CDN at the edge, where the hard problem becomes keeping caches across continents coherent — usually solved by accepting bounded staleness rather than fighting for global freshness.

chunks.title: Data modelling
chunks.text: Designing the shape of your data — the decision that quietly determines how easy or painful everything else will be. Data modelling is deciding what tables (or documents) you have, how they relate, and whether to keep data tidy and split (normalized) or duplicated for speed (denormalized) — driven by how your app will actually read and write it. Before a single query is written, someone decides the shape of the data: what entities exist (a User, an Order, a MenuProduct), what fields each holds, and how they connect. This is data modelling, and it's the most consequential design decision in the backend — get the shape wrong and every query fights it forever; get it right and most features become easy. The central tension is normalization vs denormalization. *Normalized* data stores each fact exactly once and links to it (an order points to a customer id rather than copying the customer's name). It's tidy, avoids contradictions, and is easy to update — but answering a question may require joining several tables. *Denormalized* data deliberately duplicates facts (storing the customer's name *on* the order) so a read needs no join — faster to read, but now the name lives in two places and can drift. Modelling also means picking relationships: one-to-one, one-to-many (one order, many items), and many-to-many (which needs a join table). And crucially, it means designing around your access patterns — the specific reads and writes your app does most. A model optimised for the wrong access pattern is slow no matter how elegant it looks. The data model outlives almost everything else. Code gets rewritten; the schema, once data is in it, is painful to change because every row must be migrated. A model that matches your access patterns makes features fast to build and queries fast to run; a mismatched one means awkward joins, slow reports, and contortions in every feature for years. Normalization vs denormalization is really a correctness-vs-speed dial. Normalized data can't contradict itself, which is why it's the default for anything you must trust. You denormalize *on purpose*, in specific spots, when the read speed is worth taking on the duty of keeping copies consistent — never by accident. Entities & attributes: The nouns (User, Order) and their fields — the rows and columns you'll actually store. Relationships: One-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many (via a join table) — how the nouns connect by id. Normalization: Each fact stored once, referenced by key. No duplication, no contradictions, but joins to read. Denormalization: Duplicating data to avoid joins. Faster reads, but you own keeping the copies in sync. Access patterns: The reads/writes your app does most. The model should make the common ones cheap. Relational / normalized: Tables with foreign keys, third-normal-form. The trustworthy default; joins are the price of no duplication. Denormalized / wide rows: Duplicate to avoid joins; great for read-heavy, write-light data. You own the sync burden. Document model: Store related data nested together (a JSON document). Reads of one aggregate are one fetch; cross-document joins are weak. Star schema (analytics): A deliberately denormalized shape — facts plus dimension tables — built for fast aggregation, not transactions.

chunks.title: Data modelling — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Model without thinking about access patterns and your most common query becomes a five-table join that crawls. Denormalize casually and the same customer name ends up spelled two ways in two tables with no way to know which is right. Skip foreign keys and constraints and you accumulate orphan rows — order items pointing at orders that no longer exist. Worst of all, ship the wrong model and discover it only after a million rows are in it, when fixing it means a risky, slow migration. Local: one normalized schema, a handful of tables, foreign keys and a few indexes — clean and correct. Production: the same model with carefully chosen indexes for real queries and a couple of *deliberate* denormalizations where reads proved hot. Enterprise: the transactional (OLTP) model stays normalized, while a separate denormalized warehouse (OLAP, star schema) is fed from it for analytics, so reports never touch the live model. Planet-scale: the model is shaped for sharding — chosen so the common access pattern hits a single shard — and key data is denormalized along shard boundaries to avoid cross-shard joins entirely, trading purity for the ability to grow.

chunks.title: OLTP vs OLAP
chunks.text: Why the database that takes your orders is a terrible place to run reports — and why you build a second one. OLTP systems handle the many small, fast reads and writes of running the business (placing an order); OLAP systems handle the few huge analytical scans of understanding it (last quarter's revenue by region) — and they're built so differently that you separate them. There are two utterly different jobs a database might do. OLTP — Online *Transaction* Processing — is the live workload: thousands of tiny operations like ‘insert this order', ‘read this user', ‘decrement this stock'. Each touches a few rows, must be fast and correct, and runs constantly. This is the database your app talks to. OLAP — Online *Analytical* Processing — is the opposite: a handful of enormous queries like ‘total revenue per store per month for the last two years'. Each scans millions of rows, aggregates them, and runs occasionally for a dashboard or a report. It doesn't write much; it *reads vast amounts*. The reason this matters is storage layout. OLTP databases store data row by row (the whole order together), which is perfect for ‘fetch one order'. OLAP systems store data column by column (all the revenue values together), which is perfect for ‘sum one column across millions of rows' and lets that column compress beautifully. The same data, laid out for opposite jobs — which is exactly why you can't do both well in one store. Running big analytics on your live OLTP database is the classic mistake: one heavy report scans millions of rows, saturates the database, and customers can't place orders while it runs. Separating the workloads means each runs on a system built for it, and neither starves the other. The storage layout is the deep reason they can't merge. Row stores make single-record transactions fast but column aggregations slow; column stores make aggregations fast but single-row writes slow. No single layout wins both, so the mature answer is two systems and a pipeline between them — correctness and speed on the transactional side, scale and insight on the analytical side. OLTP (transactional): Many small, fast reads/writes on a few rows each. Row-oriented storage. The live application database. OLAP (analytical): Few huge read-only scans aggregating millions of rows. Column-oriented storage. The reporting brain. Row vs column store: Rows keep a record together (fast single-record fetch); columns keep a field together (fast aggregation + compression). Data warehouse: The OLAP store (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) where historical data lands for analysis. ETL / ELT pipeline: The job that copies and reshapes OLTP data into the warehouse, on a schedule or as a stream. One database for both: Fine when tiny — run reports off-hours on the OLTP database. Stops working the moment analytics gets heavy or data gets large. Read replica for reports: Point analytics at a replica so the primary stays fast. Helps with isolation, but it's still row-oriented — big aggregations are still slow. HTAP (hybrid) systems: Newer engines that try to serve both workloads at once. Tempting, but specialised systems still win at the extremes. Column store warehouse: BigQuery/Snowflake/Redshift for OLAP. The standard once analytics matters; you accept running and feeding a second system.

chunks.title: OLTP vs OLAP — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Point the company dashboard straight at the live OLTP database and the first time someone opens it during lunch rush, every query slows and orders start timing out. Skip the warehouse and analysts write ever-heavier queries against production until one of them takes the site down. Or build the pipeline but forget it's *behind* reality, and someone treats a number that's six hours stale as live truth. Separation is what keeps fast-and-correct from colliding with big-and-insightful. Local: one database does everything; you run a report query by hand when you're curious. Production: analytics moves to a read replica so reports stop competing with checkout, though big aggregations are still slow. Enterprise: a real column-oriented warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake) fed by a nightly or streaming ETL pipeline, with a star-schema model and a BI tool on top. Planet-scale: a multi-region data platform — streaming ingestion into a sharded columnar warehouse plus a data lake of raw events — where the OLTP and OLAP worlds are entirely separate fleets, and the only thing crossing between them is the pipeline.

chunks.title: Database isolation levels
chunks.text: How much two simultaneous transactions are allowed to see of each other's half-done work — and the bugs each setting lets through. Isolation levels are the dial — from read-uncommitted up to serializable — that trades speed for safety by deciding which concurrency anomalies (dirty, non-repeatable, and phantom reads) a transaction is allowed to suffer. The I in ACID is *isolation*: the promise that concurrent transactions don't trip over each other's unfinished work. But perfect isolation is expensive, so databases offer a dial — several levels — letting you choose how much overlap you'll tolerate in exchange for more concurrency and speed. Each level is defined by which anomalies it prevents. A dirty read is seeing another transaction's write *before it commits* — it might still roll back, so you read a value that never officially existed. A non-repeatable read is reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting two different values because someone committed a change in between. A phantom read is running the same WHERE query twice and getting *different rows*, because someone inserted or deleted a row matching it. The four standard levels climb in strictness: Read Uncommitted (allows all three anomalies), Read Committed (blocks dirty reads), Repeatable Read (also blocks non-repeatable reads), and Serializable (blocks all of them — the result is *as if* the transactions ran one after another, never overlapping). Concurrency is unavoidable in any real system, and the anomalies aren't academic — a dirty read can show a balance that vanishes, a non-repeatable read can make a check pass then a write fail on stale assumptions, and a phantom can let two transactions both think they're booking the last seat. The isolation level is precisely how you decide which of these your logic must be protected from. It's a real trade-off, not a free ‘turn it to max'. Serializable everywhere serialises your throughput too — transactions wait or abort and retry, and a busy system grinds. The craft is matching the level to the stakes: Read Committed for ordinary reads, Serializable (or explicit locking) for the few operations where an anomaly would corrupt money or inventory. Read Uncommitted: Weakest. Permits dirty reads — you may see writes that later roll back. Rarely useful. Read Committed: Only see committed data. Blocks dirty reads; non-repeatable and phantom reads still possible. Postgres's default. Repeatable Read: Rows you've read won't change under you. Blocks dirty and non-repeatable reads; phantoms can still slip in (in theory). Serializable: Strongest. The outcome equals some serial order of the transactions — all three anomalies gone, at the cost of contention. The three anomalies: Dirty (uncommitted), non-repeatable (row changed mid-transaction), phantom (row set changed mid-transaction). Read Committed (default): The pragmatic baseline in Postgres/Oracle. Fast, blocks the worst anomaly (dirty reads); handle the rest case-by-case. Serializable: Correctness without thinking about anomalies — but you must retry serialization failures and accept lower throughput. Explicit row locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE to lock just the rows that matter, staying at a low level elsewhere. Surgical and common. Optimistic concurrency: A version column checked on write (see concurrency) — often a lighter alternative to high isolation for hot rows.

chunks.title: Database isolation levels — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Run a ‘check balance, then deduct' as two statements at Read Committed and two requests interleave — both read enough, both deduct, the balance goes negative. Assume Repeatable Read means your COUNT(*) is stable and a phantom row sneaks past your limit check. Crank everything to Serializable without a retry loop and the first burst of contention floods your app with unhandled serialization errors. The level you didn't think about is the anomaly that bites in production, never in testing. Local: one user, no concurrency — the level is irrelevant and the default is fine. Production: real concurrent traffic, so you keep Read Committed broadly but raise to Serializable or add FOR UPDATE locks on the handful of money/inventory operations that can't tolerate an anomaly. Enterprise: isolation choices are reviewed per critical transaction, retry-on-serialization-failure is standard middleware, and hot rows move to optimistic concurrency to dodge lock contention. Planet-scale: a single database's isolation gives way to distributed consistency — the same ‘how much can observers disagree?' question now spans regions, where true serializability across continents is so costly that systems deliberately choose weaker, bounded models.

chunks.title: Connection pooling
chunks.text: Opening a fresh database connection per request is shockingly expensive — so you keep a small set open and lend them out. A connection pool keeps a fixed number of already-open database connections ready and hands them out to requests for the moment they need one, instead of paying the heavy cost of opening and closing a connection every single time. Talking to a database isn't free to *start*: opening a connection means a TCP handshake, often a TLS handshake, then the database authenticating the user and allocating memory and a backend process for the session. That setup can take tens of milliseconds — far longer than the actual query — and the database can only hold a limited number of connections open at once before it runs out of memory. If every web request opened its own connection, did one quick query, and closed it, you'd pay that whole setup cost on every request and quickly exhaust the database's connection limit under load. A connection pool fixes this: at startup it opens a small, fixed set of connections and keeps them alive. A request borrows one, runs its query, and returns it to the pool — the connection is reused, not rebuilt. The pool has a maximum size. When all its connections are busy, a new request waits in a queue for one to free up (or times out). This is a feature, not a bug: it caps how many connections ever hit the database, turning a potential stampede into an orderly line. Pooling turns the per-request connection setup cost — the slowest part of touching the database — into a one-time startup cost. Reusing warm connections can be the difference between a query taking 2ms and 40ms, and it's often the single biggest, cheapest latency win in a backend. Just as importantly, the pool protects the database. A database has a strict ceiling on concurrent connections, and blowing past it brings the whole thing down for everyone. By capping connections at the pool's max and queueing the rest, the pool converts a traffic spike from a database-killing stampede into a manageable wait — backpressure, applied right at the data layer. Pool size (min/max): How many connections are kept open. Max caps the load on the database; min keeps some always warm. Acquire / release: A request borrows a connection to run its query, then must return it — forgetting to is a leak. Wait queue & timeout: When all connections are busy, requests queue; an acquire-timeout stops them waiting forever. Idle & max-lifetime: Connections idle too long are closed; old ones are recycled, so the pool stays healthy. Health checks: The pool validates a connection is still alive before lending it, dropping dead ones quietly. Connection per request: Open and close every time. Simple, but pays full setup cost per request and exhausts the database under load. One shared connection: Reuse a single connection everywhere. No setup cost, but it serialises all queries and breaks under concurrency. External pooler (PgBouncer): A dedicated process pooling connections in front of Postgres — essential when many app instances each have their own pool. Serverless data proxy: Managed pooling (RDS Proxy, Prisma Accelerate) for serverless functions that spin up too fast to hold a normal pool.

chunks.title: Connection pooling — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Set the pool too large and every app instance opens dozens of connections; ten instances and you've blown past Postgres's connection limit, refusing all new connections site-wide. Set it too small and requests queue behind a starved pool, adding latency that looks like a slow database but is really a slow *wait for a connection*. Forget to release a connection — leak it in an error path — and the pool slowly drains until nothing can talk to the database at all. And in serverless, where functions spin up faster than connections can be reused, a naive pool can exhaust the database in seconds without an external pooler. Local: a tiny pool (a handful of connections) inside your one app process is plenty and invisible. Production: a tuned pool per app instance, sized against the database's connection cap, with acquire-timeouts so a saturated pool fails fast instead of hanging. Enterprise: many app instances mean an external pooler (PgBouncer) in front of the database does transaction-level pooling, so thousands of app-side ‘connections' fold down to a safe few hundred real ones. Planet-scale: regional databases each fronted by their own pooler tier, with serverless workloads routed through managed data proxies — the entire architecture organised around the truth that real database connections are a scarce, precious resource.

chunks.title: Webhooks
chunks.text: Don't keep asking ‘did it happen yet?' — let the other system call you the instant it does. A webhook is a URL you register with another system so that, when an event happens there (a payment succeeds), it sends an HTTP request *to you* — push instead of poll — and the engineering is all in making that delivery reliable, verified, and safe to retry. Often your system needs to know when something happens in *another* system — a payment provider confirms a charge, a shipping service marks a parcel delivered. The naive way is polling: ask ‘is it done yet?' every few seconds. That's wasteful (most answers are ‘not yet') and slow (you learn late). A webhook flips it: you give the other system a URL of yours, and *it* makes an HTTP POST to that URL the moment the event occurs. So a webhook is just an HTTP endpoint you expose, and the other system is the client calling it. Stripe finishes a payment → it POSTs a JSON event to https://yourapp.com/webhooks/stripe. You're now the *server* receiving someone else's *push*. The whole difficulty of webhooks is reliability and trust, because the call comes from outside. The network is flaky, so deliveries get retried — meaning the same event can arrive twice, so your handler must be idempotent. And anyone on the internet can POST to your URL, so you must verify the request really came from the sender (via a signature) before you believe a word of it. Webhooks exist because polling doesn't scale and isn't timely: you'd either ask too often (wasting both systems' resources on ‘not yet') or too rarely (learning about the payment minutes late). Push delivery is instant and cheap — the sender does the work of telling you, exactly once per event, the moment it matters. The reliability machinery — signing, retries, idempotency — isn't optional ceremony; it's the cost of accepting a call from outside your trust boundary. Skip the signature and you'll act on forged events; skip idempotency and a routine retry will double-process a real one. Webhooks are easy to *receive* and genuinely hard to receive *correctly*. Registered URL: The endpoint you give the sender; where it POSTs events. Often configurable per event type. Event payload: The JSON the sender POSTs — what happened, when, and the data — usually with an event id. Signature & secret: A hash of the payload signed with a shared secret, so you can prove the request is genuine and untampered. Retries & acks: You return 2xx to acknowledge; if you don't, the sender retries with backoff — so events can repeat. Idempotency key: The event id you record once-processed, so a re-delivered event is recognised and skipped. Polling: Repeatedly ask the other system for status. Dead simple, no public endpoint needed; wasteful and laggy at any real frequency. WebSockets / SSE: A held-open connection for a continuous stream of events to a client. Great for live UI; heavier than a webhook for occasional server-to-server events. Message queue / event bus: If both systems share infrastructure, publish to a queue instead of HTTP — more reliable, but requires shared plumbing. Polling a changes feed: Pull a cursor-based ‘what changed since X' endpoint. A robust middle ground when webhooks aren't offered.

chunks.title: Webhooks — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Trust the payload without verifying the signature and an attacker POSTs a fake ‘payment succeeded' to your URL and gets free product. Skip idempotency and a perfectly normal retry processes the same order twice — a double charge or double fulfilment. Do slow work *before* returning 2xx and the sender times out, retries, and now you've got pile-ups and duplicates from your own slowness. Verify the signature against the *parsed* body instead of the raw bytes and valid events start failing mysteriously. Every one of these is a webhook handler that ‘worked in testing'. Local: one endpoint behind a tunnel, processing events inline, logging as you go — fine for development. Production: verify every signature, return 2xx immediately and hand the event to a background queue, and dedupe by event id so retries are safe. Enterprise: a dedicated webhook-ingestion service fronting all providers, recording every raw event, enforcing idempotency centrally, and replaying failed deliveries from a dead-letter queue. Planet-scale: regional ingestion endpoints behind a gateway absorbing millions of events, persisting them durably the instant they arrive, then fanning the work out to many idempotent workers — and on the *sending* side, your own outbound-webhook system with per-subscriber retry, backoff, and signing.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Cloud networking — VPCs, subnets, security groups
chunks.title: Cloud networking — VPCs, subnets, security groups
chunks.text: Building a private, walled-off network inside someone else's data center — and deciding exactly what can talk to what. Cloud networking is the private network you carve out in the cloud (a VPC), split into subnets, fenced by security groups, and fronted by load balancers — so your servers can reach each other but the internet only reaches what you choose to expose. When you rent servers in the cloud they don't just float on the open internet — you place them inside a VPC (Virtual Private Cloud): your own isolated slice of the provider's network, with a private address range (like 10.0.0.0/16) that nobody else can see or route to. It feels like your company's office network, except it lives in a rented data center. Inside the VPC you carve out subnets — smaller address ranges, usually one per availability zone. The crucial split is public subnets (machines that may receive internet traffic, like a load balancer) versus private subnets (databases and app servers that should never be directly reachable from outside). A machine in a private subnet can call out, but the internet cannot call in. What's actually *allowed* to flow is decided by security groups — per-machine firewalls that say ‘accept traffic on port 443 from anywhere, port 5432 only from the app servers'. They default to ‘deny everything', so you open holes deliberately. In front of it all sits a load balancer, the one public door that spreads incoming requests across your private app servers. The alternative — every server with a public IP and a hand-managed firewall — means one misconfigured machine is directly exposed to the entire internet, and there's no clean boundary to reason about. A VPC gives you a *default-private* posture: nothing is reachable until you deliberately route and open it, which is exactly the right default for security. It also makes the network match the architecture. Tiers (web / app / data) map to subnets and security groups, so ‘the database is only reachable by the app' stops being a hope and becomes an enforced rule. And spreading subnets across availability zones is what makes the whole system survive losing a data center. VPC: Your isolated private network with its own address range; the boundary everything else lives inside. Subnet: A slice of the VPC, tied to one availability zone. Public ones face the internet; private ones don't. Security group: A per-resource firewall: a list of which ports accept traffic, and from which sources. Default-deny. Load balancer: The public entry point that spreads incoming requests across healthy app servers in private subnets. NAT & gateways: A NAT gateway lets private machines reach *out* (for updates) without being reachable *in*; an internet gateway connects public subnets. Flat public networking: Give every box a public IP and a firewall. Simple for one server, a sprawling attack surface as you grow. Service mesh / private links: Push connectivity and policy *between* services (sidecars, private endpoints); complements the VPC rather than replacing it. Provider default VPC: Every account ships with a default VPC so you can start instantly — fine for experiments, too permissive for production. Zero-trust networking: Stop trusting the network at all — authenticate every call regardless of where it came from. The modern direction; more work to adopt.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Cloud networking — VPCs, subnets, security groups
chunks.title: Cloud networking — VPCs, subnets, security groups — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Put a database in a public subnet ‘just to test' and you've exposed it to the whole internet — a classic breach origin. Open a security group to 0.0.0.0/0 on the wrong port and the firewall is decorative. Forget that security groups are default-deny and your services silently can't reach each other, with no error pointing at the network. Stuff everything in one subnet in one availability zone and a single data-center outage takes you fully down. The discipline: default-private, least-privilege groups, and multi-AZ from day one. Local: no network at all — everything talks over localhost on your laptop. Production: one VPC, public and private subnets across two availability zones, security groups enforcing web→app→data, a load balancer out front. Enterprise: many VPCs (per team, per environment) peered or hub-and-spoked together, centralized egress and inspection, private links to managed services so traffic never touches the public internet. Planet-scale: VPCs in every region, global load balancing steering users to the nearest one, and a zero-trust overlay where the network is no longer trusted on its own — every call is authenticated end to end.

chunks.title: Edge computing
chunks.text: Running your code on servers close to the user instead of in one far-away data center — so the round-trip is short. Edge computing moves computation out to the hundreds of points-of-presence near users (the same network that powers CDNs), so the work happens metres away instead of an ocean away — turning a CDN from something that only caches into something that also computes. A normal app runs in one (or a few) data centers. A user in Sydney calling a server in Virginia eats a ~200ms round-trip *per request*, no matter how fast the server is — the speed of light is the bottleneck. Edge computing fixes this by running your code in the points-of-presence (PoPs) a CDN already operates all over the world, so the user is served from a machine in their own city. You already met this network as a CDN that *caches* static files near users. Edge computing is the next step: the same edge nodes can now *run logic* — rewrite a request, check an auth token, personalize a page, do an A/B split, call a nearby database — not just hand back a cached file. The edge stops being a dumb cache and becomes a thin compute layer. Edge runtimes are deliberately constrained: tiny, fast-starting environments (often based on V8 isolates rather than full containers) with strict CPU and memory limits and no long-lived local disk. You trade the power of a full server for the ability to run *everywhere at once*, instantly, with no cold-start penalty worth mentioning. Latency is felt, not measured — a page that responds in 50ms feels alive while one at 300ms feels sluggish, and for a global audience the *distance* dominates that number. Doing auth checks, redirects, personalization, and caching at the edge cuts the round-trips that matter most, and it offloads the origin so your central servers do far less work. It also improves resilience and cost: the edge absorbs traffic spikes and attacks before they reach your origin, and serving from a nearby cache is far cheaper than recomputing in one region for the whole planet. The trade is a constrained runtime and a harder mental model — your code now runs in many places with no shared memory. Point-of-presence (PoP): An edge location near users — the same global footprint a CDN uses to cache files. Edge function: A small, fast-starting piece of code (V8 isolate / WASM) that runs at the PoP on each request. Edge cache: The original CDN job — storing responses near users — now programmable from your edge code. Origin: Your real backend in a central region; the edge calls it only when it can't answer locally. Edge data: Replicated key-value stores at the edge so functions can read config or session data without a long trip to origin. Central region only: Run everything in one place. Simplest to reason about; distant users pay the round-trip on every request. Multi-region origin: Full backends in several regions. More power than the edge, far more cost and operational complexity to keep in sync. Plain CDN (cache only): Cache static files near users but compute nothing. Great for assets; can't personalize or run logic. Client-side logic: Push work into the browser instead of the edge. No server cost, but limited by the device and unsafe for secrets.

chunks.title: Edge computing — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Treat an edge function like a full server — pull in a heavy library or do a long computation — and it blows the CPU/memory budget and fails under load. Assume local state persists between requests and you get baffling bugs, because the next request may hit a different PoP entirely. Forget that the edge still has to call origin for writes and you build something ‘fast' that's actually slow on every write. Cache personalized content at the edge by mistake and one user sees another's data. The edge rewards small, stateless, read-mostly logic and punishes everything else. Local: there is no edge — your function runs once, on your laptop. Production: a single managed edge function (Workers/Vercel Edge) handling redirects, auth checks, and caching in front of one central origin. Enterprise: many edge functions across PoPs running personalization, A/B tests, and geo-routing, with edge-replicated config and a central origin per region behind them. Planet-scale: the edge becomes a real compute tier — hundreds of PoPs, edge-resident data stores, requests resolved entirely at the edge for the common case, and the origin reduced to the system of record that the edge only occasionally consults.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Stream processing — batch vs stream
chunks.title: Stream processing — batch vs stream
chunks.text: Processing events the moment they arrive, continuously, instead of collecting them and crunching the pile later. Stream processing handles data as an unbounded, never-ending flow — computing results over rolling time windows as each event lands — where batch processing waits, collects a finite chunk, and processes it all at once. There are two fundamentally different ways to process data. Batch processing collects a *bounded* set — yesterday's orders, this month's logs — and runs a job over the whole pile at once: simple, efficient, but the answer is always as old as the batch interval. Stream processing treats data as an *unbounded* flow and computes results continuously, updating as each new event arrives, so the answer is always seconds fresh. The hard part of streaming is that the data never ends, so ‘compute the total' is meaningless — total *over what*? The answer is windows: you slice the endless stream into chunks of time. A tumbling window is fixed, non-overlapping buckets (‘count per minute'); a sliding window overlaps (‘count over the last 5 minutes, updated every minute'); a session window groups bursts of activity separated by gaps. Two notions of time make it subtle. Event time is when something actually happened; processing time is when your system saw it. Events arrive late and out of order (a phone was offline), so a good stream processor waits a bounded grace period — tracked by a watermark — before declaring a window closed, balancing freshness against correctness. Batch is fine when ‘yesterday's numbers' are good enough — billing, reporting, training a model. But fraud detection, live dashboards, alerting, and personalization need the answer *now*, and re-running a batch every few seconds is wasteful and still laggy. Streaming computes incrementally on each event, so latency drops from hours to milliseconds and you do far less redundant work. The cost is real complexity: out-of-order data, exactly-once semantics, state that must be checkpointed, and windows you have to reason about carefully. Many mature systems run *both* — a streaming path for fresh-but-approximate answers and a batch path for complete-but-late ground truth — which is the heart of the lambda/kappa architecture debate. Unbounded stream: A never-ending sequence of events (clicks, sensor readings, orders) processed as it flows, not collected first. Window: A slice of the stream by time — tumbling (fixed), sliding (overlapping), or session (gap-delimited) — that gives ‘over what' an answer. Event time vs processing time: When it happened vs when you saw it. Late, out-of-order arrivals make these diverge. Watermark: A moving ‘we've probably seen everything up to time T' marker that decides when a window is safe to close. State & checkpointing: Running aggregates the processor keeps in memory, snapshotted periodically so it can recover exactly where it left off after a crash. Batch processing: Collect a finite chunk and process it all at once. Simpler and cheaper per record; always as stale as the interval. Micro-batch: Tiny, frequent batches (e.g. every few seconds) that approximate streaming with simpler mechanics; Spark's classic model. Database triggers / CDC: React to row changes in a database directly. Fine for modest volumes; doesn't scale to high-throughput event flows. Request-time computation: Don't pre-process at all — compute on read. Simplest, but slow and expensive for heavy aggregations under load.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Stream processing — batch vs stream
chunks.title: Stream processing — batch vs stream — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Pick processing time instead of event time and your ‘per-minute' counts smear whenever ingestion lags — the numbers become meaningless during a backlog. Set the watermark too tight and you silently drop every late event; too loose and your dashboards lag. Forget checkpointing and a single crash either loses results or double-counts them. Let per-key state grow without bound (a window that never closes, a key that never expires) and the processor runs out of memory. Streaming is powerful only when time semantics, watermarks, and state lifetime are chosen deliberately. Local: a single-threaded loop reading events from a file and bucketing them by minute — streaming in miniature. Production: one stream-processing job (Flink/Kafka Streams) reading a topic, computing windowed aggregates with checkpointing to recover from crashes, writing results to a database. Enterprise: many jobs across a managed cluster, partitioned by key for parallelism, with exactly-once sinks into a warehouse and careful watermark tuning per source. Planet-scale: globally distributed pipelines ingesting millions of events per second, regional processors with cross-region state replication, and a blended batch+stream architecture so live answers and complete answers coexist.

chunks.title: ETL & data pipelines
chunks.text: The plumbing that moves data out of the systems that produce it, reshapes it, and lands it where analysts and models can use it. An ETL pipeline extracts data from source systems, transforms it into a clean, consistent shape, and loads it into a destination (usually a warehouse) — orchestrated as a dependency graph of steps that runs on a schedule or in response to events. Data is born scattered — in your app's database, in third-party APIs, in log files, in spreadsheets — and in shapes built for *transactions*, not *analysis*. A pipeline is the repeatable process that collects it, cleans and reshapes it, and delivers it somewhere useful. The classic name is ETL: Extract from the sources, Transform into a clean model, Load into the destination. A newer ordering, ELT (Extract, Load, Transform), flips the last two: dump the raw data into a powerful warehouse *first*, then transform it *inside* the warehouse using SQL. This won out for cloud warehouses because their compute is cheap and elastic — it's easier to load everything raw and transform later than to perfectly shape it in flight, and you keep the raw data for re-processing. The transform step is where the real work lives: deduplicating, fixing types and time zones, joining sources, handling nulls, and modeling the data (e.g. into facts and dimensions). And because real pipelines have many interdependent steps, they're expressed as a DAG (directed acyclic graph) — step B runs only after step A succeeds — and run by an orchestrator that schedules, retries, and monitors them. Without a pipeline, analysts query the production database directly — slowing the app, seeing transaction-shaped data that's painful to analyze, and getting inconsistent answers because everyone cleans it differently.
