You push items on the top and pop them off the top, so the last thing you added is the first thing you get back. Think of a stack of plates: you take the top one. A queue is FIFO — *first in, first out*. You enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front, so items are served in the order they arrived. Think of a checkout line: first to arrive, first to be served. You don't usually access the middle of either — you only ever touch the one end the rule allows. That restriction is the point: by giving up random access, you get a structure that perfectly captures ‘undo the most recent thing' (stack) or ‘handle things fairly in arrival order' (queue). These exist because order-of-handling is a real, recurring need, and these two rules cover most of it. ‘Undo' is a stack (reverse the most recent action). A web server's incoming requests are a queue (serve them fairly). A maze solver explores with a stack (depth-first) or a queue (breadth-first) — same maze, different rule, different search. The trade-off is deliberate poverty: you can't peek in the middle or grab an arbitrary item. If you need that, you've outgrown a stack/queue and want a different structure. Their *whole value* is the discipline of the single allowed end. Stack — LIFO: Push/pop at one end. Models ‘most recent first': undo, back button, function calls. Queue — FIFO: Enqueue at back, dequeue at front. Models ‘fair, in order': print jobs, task lines, requests. The call stack: How your program tracks which function is running — a stack the language manages for you. Deque: A double-ended queue: add/remove at *both* ends. A flexible superset of both. Priority queue (heap): When ‘who's next' isn't oldest or newest but *most important*. A queue that serves by priority, not arrival. Deque: When you need both ends. Built-in in most languages; can act as either a stack or a queue. Plain array/list: When you actually need to read the middle or jump around — then the stack/queue restriction is just in your way.

chunks.title: Stacks & queues — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Pop from an empty stack or dequeue an empty queue and you get a crash or nonsense if you didn't check first. The famous one is the stack overflow: a recursion that never stops keeps pushing call frames until the call stack runs out of room and the program dies — the call stack is finite, and forgetting that is a rite of passage. In-memory: trivially fast at any size that fits in RAM. As a system grows, the *queue* idea graduates to durable, distributed message queues (Kafka, SQS) that hold millions of jobs across machines and survive crashes — but the FIFO promise you learn here is exactly what they're keeping. Stacks stay mostly a local, in-process tool.

chunks.title: Hash tables & maps
chunks.text: Look something up by name in one step — the closest thing in computing to instant magic. A hash table stores key–value pairs and finds any value by its key in roughly one step, by turning the key into an array position with a hash function. A hash table (you'll also hear map, dictionary, or hash map — same thing) stores pairs: a key and its value. Give it the key ‘user_42' and it hands back that user's record — *without searching*. That near-instant lookup-by-name is its whole reason to exist, and it's one of the most useful structures in all of computing. The trick is the hash function: a little routine that takes your key and scrambles it into a number — an index into an internal array of buckets. Store ‘user_42 → record' and the hash function decides ‘that lives in bucket 9'. Later, to look it up, it runs the *same* key through the *same* hash function, gets bucket 9 again, and grabs the value. No scanning — it computed exactly where to look. That's O(1) average time: constant, no matter how many items you've stored. Sometimes two different keys hash to the *same* bucket — that's a collision. It's expected and handled: typically the bucket holds a tiny list, and the table checks the few keys there. Done well, collisions stay rare, so lookups stay effectively one step. Hash tables are the go-to whenever you need ‘fetch the thing associated with *this* key, fast' — counting how many times each word appears, remembering which ids you've already seen, caching computed answers, or de-duplicating a list. They routinely turn an O(n) scan into an O(1) lookup, which is the single most common performance win a programmer reaches for. The cost of that speed: a hash table has no order. It can't tell you the smallest key, or everything between two keys, or what comes ‘next' — the hashing deliberately scatters keys. When you need order or range queries, that's exactly when you reach for a tree instead. Key & value: You store and fetch the value *by* its key. The key is your handle on the data. Hash function: Turns a key into a bucket number, fast and consistently. The heart of the structure. Buckets: Slots in an internal array where pairs land. Ideally one or two items each. Collision handling: What to do when two keys share a bucket — keep a small list there, or probe nearby. Balanced tree (BST): When you need keys kept in sorted order or range queries. O(log n) lookups instead of O(1), but ordered. Array: When your ‘key' is already a small integer position. Then a plain array *is* a perfect O(1) map. Trie: For string keys where you also want prefix search (autocomplete). Specialised, but powerful for text.

chunks.title: Hash tables & maps — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: A bad hash function that piles most keys into a few buckets degrades the whole table to a linear scan — O(1) quietly becomes O(n) and nobody notices until it's slow. Worse, an attacker who knows your hash can *deliberately* cause collisions to grind your server to a halt (a real denial-of-service attack). And reaching for a hash table when you actually needed sorted order means re-sorting the keys every single time — the wrong tool fighting you. In memory: superb up to whatever fits in RAM. Bigger: the table resizes itself; the only cost is the occasional rehash. Beyond one machine: keys are partitioned across servers by hash (a distributed hash table / consistent hashing), which is precisely how sharding decides which database holds which user. The same idea you learn here scales from a 10-line script to a planet-spanning store.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Trees & binary search trees
chunks.title: Trees & binary search trees
chunks.text: Branching structures for anything with a hierarchy — and, kept sorted, for halving a search at every step. A tree links nodes in a parent-child hierarchy; a binary search tree keeps them ordered so you can find any value by repeatedly halving the search. A tree is a structure of nodes connected in a hierarchy: one root node at the top, each node pointing to its children below, branching downward with no loops. A node with no children is a leaf. Trees are how computers model anything nested — a file system (folders inside folders), a web page (tags inside tags), a company org chart, a comment thread. A binary search tree (BST) is a special, *ordered* tree where each node has at most two children and obeys one rule: everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node, and everything in the right is larger. That single rule turns the tree into a searching machine. To find a value, you start at the root and compare: smaller? go left. Larger? go right. Each step throws away half the remaining tree. Halving at every step is what makes a BST fast: searching a million sorted items takes about 20 comparisons, not a million. That ‘halve each time' cost is called O(log n) — logarithmic time — and it's the sweet spot between the instant-but-unordered hash table and the slow linear scan. Trees exist for two big reasons. First, hierarchy is everywhere — folders, the DOM, menus, org charts — and a tree is its natural shape. Second, a balanced BST gives you something a hash table can't: sorted order with fast lookup. You can ask for the smallest key, everything between two values, or the next-largest — *range queries* — while still finding any single item in O(log n). The trade-off versus a hash table is one step slower for a plain lookup (log n vs constant), in exchange for keeping everything ordered. That ordering is so valuable that the most important tree of all — the B-tree — is what every database uses for its indexes, because ‘find this row fast' and ‘give me all rows between two dates' both fall out of it. Root, child, leaf: Top node, the nodes hanging off it, and the nodes with nothing below them. The BST rule: Left subtree < node < right subtree. This ordering is what enables fast search. Height & balance: How many levels deep. A *balanced* tree stays shallow, which keeps search at O(log n). Self-balancing trees: Red-black & AVL trees re-shuffle on insert so the tree never degenerates into a slow line. Hash table: Faster for a single lookup (O(1)) but unordered. Pick the tree when you need sorting or ranges. B-tree / B+ tree: A wide, shallow tree tuned for disk — the structure behind virtually every database index. Trie: A tree keyed by the characters of strings — ideal for prefix search and autocomplete.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Trees & binary search trees
chunks.title: Trees & binary search trees — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Insert already-sorted data into a plain BST and it silently degenerates into a slow line — your O(log n) lookups become O(n) and you won't see why until it's slow at scale. That exact failure is the reason self-balancing trees exist. Traversal bugs bite too: get the recursion wrong and you visit nodes twice, skip a subtree, or loop forever. Small: any tree works. Large in memory: use a self-balancing BST so it never degenerates. Data too big for memory: that's where B-trees shine — wide and shallow to minimise slow disk reads, which is exactly how databases index billions of rows. Planet-scale: those B-tree indexes get replicated and sharded, but the halving-the-search idea you learn here is still doing the work.

chunks.title: Graphs
chunks.text: Dots joined by lines — the structure for anything where ‘things are connected to things'. A graph is a set of nodes connected by edges; it models networks — friends, roads, dependencies — and you explore it with BFS or DFS. A graph is the most general structure of all: a set of nodes (also called *vertices* — the dots) joined by edges (the lines between them). Unlike a tree, there's no root and no rule against loops — any node can connect to any other. That freedom is exactly what lets a graph model the messy, interconnected real world. Edges can be undirected (a two-way friendship: if A knows B, B knows A) or directed (a one-way link: A follows B, but not back). They can also be weighted — carrying a number like distance, cost, or time (the 12 km between two towns). Pick those options and a graph can represent a social network, a road map, the web's links, task dependencies, or which airports connect to which. Because a graph has no fixed starting point or shape, the fundamental operation is traversal — systematically visiting nodes by following edges. The two classic ways are BFS (breadth-first: explore everything one step away, then two steps, like ripples) and DFS (depth-first: charge as far down one path as you can, then back up and try another). Graphs exist because *connection* is one of the most common things we model, and trees and lists are too rigid for it. Anything shaped like a network — friends, followers, roads, flights, web links, ‘which task must finish before which' — is a graph, and the questions you ask (is there a path? what's the shortest one? who's most central? is there a cycle?) are graph algorithms. The trade-off is that graphs are heavier to reason about than their simpler cousins. There's no neat ordering to exploit, traversals must guard against cycles, and the richest questions (shortest path, best matching) get genuinely intricate. You take on that complexity precisely when the problem really is a network and nothing simpler will capture it. Nodes & edges: The dots and the connections between them. The two raw ingredients. Directed / weighted: Are links one-way or two-way? Do they carry a cost (distance, time)? These choices model reality. BFS — breadth-first: Explore in rings, nearest first. Uses a queue. Finds the fewest-hops path. DFS — depth-first: Follow one path to its end, then backtrack. Uses a stack (or recursion). Great for ‘is there a path?' and cycles. Tree: A graph with no cycles and a single root. Simpler — use it when your data is a clean hierarchy, not a web. Adjacency list vs matrix: List for sparse graphs (few edges), matrix for small/dense ones. The storage choice changes performance. Graph database: Neo4j and friends store relationships as first-class data — when connections, not rows, are the whole point.

chunks.title: Graphs — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Forget the ‘visited' set and a traversal walks in circles forever on a cycle — the program hangs, never finishing. Choose the wrong storage (a matrix for a huge, sparse social graph) and you blow up memory. And reaching for a heavy graph algorithm when the data was really a simple tree or list just buries a simple problem under needless complexity. Small graphs: traverse freely in memory. Large (millions of nodes): the algorithm and storage choice decide whether it finishes in milliseconds or never — adjacency lists and good pruning matter. Planet-scale graphs (a global social network): they're partitioned across thousands of machines, traversed with distributed and approximate algorithms, and often kept in dedicated graph databases. The nodes-and-edges idea is the same; the engineering to traverse billions of them is immense.

chunks.title: Heaps & priority queues
chunks.text: A line where the most urgent item always jumps to the front — and getting it is instant. A heap is a tree that always keeps its smallest (or largest) item at the top, giving you instant access to the most extreme element. A priority queue is like an ordinary queue, but instead of serving items by arrival order, it always serves the most important one next — the ambulance jumps the traffic. You put items in (each with a priority), and every time you take one out, you get the current highest priority. The structure that makes this efficient is the heap. A heap is a special tree with one simple promise, the heap property: every parent is smaller than its children (a min-heap) — or larger (a max-heap). That promise means the smallest (or largest) item is *always sitting at the root*, so peeking at the most extreme element is instant, O(1). Adding an item or removing the top costs only O(log n) — the height of the tree. Cleverly, a heap doesn't need real tree nodes and pointers. Because it's always a neat, filled-in shape (a *complete* tree), it's stored as a plain array, with simple arithmetic to find a node's children and parent. So you get tree-like behaviour with array-like efficiency and no pointer bookkeeping. Heaps exist for the surprisingly common need: *‘give me the most extreme item right now, and keep that true as items come and go.'* A plain sorted list could answer ‘what's the smallest?' but every insert would cost O(n) to keep it sorted; a heap keeps inserts at O(log n) while still surfacing the extreme instantly. That balance is why it's the standard tool for ‘top-K', schedulers, and shortest-path search. The trade-off: a heap only ever tells you about the *one* extreme. It is not fully sorted — the items below the root are in a loose, partial order, so you can't ask ‘what's the 5th smallest?' or list everything in order without popping. If you need full ordering or range queries, you want a sorted structure or a tree instead. Heap property: Every parent beats its children (smaller for min-heap, larger for max-heap). Keeps the extreme at the root. Peek — O(1): The min (or max) is always the root, so reading it is instant. Insert & pop — O(log n): Add or remove the top, then ‘bubble' the heap back into shape — only as far as the tree is tall. Array-backed: Stored as a flat array (no pointers); children of index i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2. Sorted array/list: Always fully ordered and O(1) to read the min — but O(n) to insert. Good when inserts are rare. Balanced BST: Gives the min/max *and* full ordering and ranges, at O(log n) — more power, slightly more overhead. Plain queue: When ‘next' really is just oldest-first and priority doesn't matter, skip the heap entirely.

chunks.title: Heaps & priority queues — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Treat a heap as if it were fully sorted and you'll get nonsense — only the root is guaranteed; the rest is partially ordered, so iterating the array is *not* iterating in order. Mix up a min-heap and a max-heap and your ‘most urgent' becomes your least urgent. And forgetting that the heap only exposes the top leads people to rebuild or re-sort it constantly, throwing away the very efficiency they came for. In memory: excellent into the millions for ‘top-K' and scheduling. Bigger than memory or across machines: the *idea* persists in distributed schedulers and priority job queues, though keeping a single global priority order across many servers gets genuinely hard (and is often relaxed to ‘roughly prioritised'). The core bubble-up/sink-down logic, though, is exactly what you learn here.

chunks.title: Recursion & backtracking
chunks.text: A function that calls itself to solve a smaller version of its own problem — until the problem is trivial. Recursion solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece and combining the results; backtracking adds ‘try a choice, and undo it if it fails'. Recursion is a function that calls itself. It sounds circular, but it works because each call tackles a *smaller* version of the same problem, and there's a base case — a smallest version simple enough to answer directly, with no further calls. Reach the base case and the chain of calls unwinds, combining results back up to the original question. Every correct recursion has two parts. The base case: ‘if the problem is trivial, here's the answer outright' (an empty list sums to 0; a folder with no subfolders has only its own files). The recursive case: ‘otherwise, solve a smaller piece by calling myself, and build my answer from that' (the sum of a list is its first item plus *the sum of the rest*). Get the base case wrong and the function never stops. Backtracking is recursion with choices and an eraser. At each step you *try* an option, recurse to see if it leads to a solution, and if it hits a dead end you undo that choice and try the next. It's how you explore every possibility methodically — solving a maze, a Sudoku, or arranging items — without getting lost: go forward while you can, step back the moment you're stuck. Recursion is the natural language for anything self-similar — a structure made of smaller copies of itself. Trees, nested folders, parsing nested brackets, divide-and-conquer algorithms like merge sort: writing these recursively is often *dramatically* shorter and clearer than the loop-based equivalent, because the code mirrors the shape of the data. The trade-off is real, though. Every call costs a stack frame, so recursion uses more memory than a loop and can overflow the stack if it goes too deep. Anything recursive can be rewritten with a loop and an explicit stack — sometimes you should, for speed or depth. Recursion is a tool for clarity on self-similar problems, not a hammer for everything. Base case: The smallest problem you answer directly, with no further recursion. Without it, infinite calls. Recursive case: Solve a smaller sub-problem by calling yourself, then build your answer from it. The call stack: Each call is a frame pushed on the stack; reaching the base case pops back up. This *is* the mechanism. Backtracking: Make a choice, recurse, and undo it if it leads to a dead end — exploring all options safely. Iteration (loops): Often faster and won't overflow the stack. Preferred for simple repetition; clunky for deeply nested structures. Explicit stack: Rewrite a recursion as a loop that manages its own stack — the depth safety of iteration with recursion's reach. Memoised recursion: Cache results of repeated sub-calls — the doorway to dynamic programming, turning exponential into fast.

chunks.title: Recursion & backtracking — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Forget or botch the base case and the function calls itself forever, piling frames onto the call stack until it runs out of room — the dreaded stack overflow, and your program dies. Recurse too deep on big input (a 100,000-level structure) and you overflow even *with* a correct base case. And naive recursion that re-solves the same sub-problem millions of times (plain Fibonacci) can be astronomically slow — the cue to add memoisation. Fine for modest depth. Deep recursion needs care: convert to iteration with an explicit stack, or use ‘tail-call' tricks where the language supports them, to avoid blowing the stack. At large scale the recursive *idea* — divide a problem into smaller identical pieces — is exactly how big distributed jobs split work (map-reduce is divide-and-conquer across machines), even when no single function literally calls itself.

chunks.title: Dynamic programming
chunks.text: Solve each little sub-problem once, write the answer down, and never compute it twice. Dynamic programming speeds up problems that re-solve the same sub-problems by storing each answer the first time and reusing it. Dynamic programming (DP) has an intimidating name and a simple core: *don't solve the same thing twice*. It applies to problems that, when you break them down, keep bumping into the same smaller sub-problems over and over. DP solves each sub-problem once, stores the answer, and looks it up instead of recomputing — turning work that explodes exponentially into something fast. Two ingredients tell you DP fits. Overlapping sub-problems: the naive (usually recursive) solution computes the same sub-answers again and again — classic Fibonacci recomputes fib(5) a staggering number of times. Optimal substructure: the best answer to the whole is built from the best answers to its parts (the cheapest route through a grid is built from the cheapest routes to the cells before it). When both hold, DP is the tool. There are two styles. Memoisation (top-down): write the natural recursion, but cache each result in a table the first time you compute it, and return the cache on repeat calls. Tabulation (bottom-up): fill a table starting from the smallest sub-problems and build up to the answer with a loop. Same idea — compute each cell once — from opposite directions. DP exists to rescue problems that are *correct* but hopelessly *slow* when solved naively. Many optimisation questions — shortest paths, ‘fewest coins to make this amount', ‘longest common subsequence' between two texts, knapsack-style ‘best value under a limit' — have a clean recursive definition that, run literally, would take longer than the age of the universe because it redoes the same work astronomically often. DP makes them run in milliseconds. The trade-off is memory and insight. You spend extra space on the table of stored answers (sometimes reducible with cleverness), and — the real cost — DP is *hard to see*. Recognising that a problem has overlapping sub-problems, and defining the sub-problem and its combining rule correctly, is a genuine skill that takes practice. It is famously the most feared topic in coding interviews for exactly this reason. Overlapping sub-problems: The same smaller problems recur many times — the signal that caching will pay off hugely. Optimal substructure: The best whole-answer is built from best sub-answers. Lets you combine pieces correctly. Memoisation (top-down): Keep the recursion, but store each result in a table and reuse it on repeat calls. Tabulation (bottom-up): Fill a table from smallest sub-problem upward with a loop — no recursion, no stack risk. Plain recursion: Simpler to write, but recomputes everything — fine only when sub-problems *don't* overlap. Greedy algorithm: Make the locally best choice each step. Faster and simpler when it works — but it doesn't always give the true optimum; DP does. Memoisation vs tabulation: Two ways to do DP itself: top-down caching (easier to write) vs bottom-up table (no stack risk, often faster).

chunks.title: Dynamic programming — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Apply DP where sub-problems *don't* actually overlap and you've added a useless table — extra memory for nothing. Define the sub-problem wrong and the table gives confidently incorrect answers that are painful to debug. And forgetting the cache (writing the recursion but never storing results) leaves you with the original exponential blow-up — the slow version wearing DP's clothes. Single machine: a well-built DP solves inputs that would otherwise be impossible. As inputs grow, the table itself can get huge, so engineers shrink it (keeping only the last row, say) or switch to streaming. At very large scale the principle — *don't recompute; remember* — reappears as caching layers and precomputed results across a whole system, the same instinct you learned here applied to infrastructure.

chunks.title: Sorting & searching
chunks.text: Put things in order, then find any of them in a handful of steps — the two oldest tricks in the book, still everywhere. Sorting arranges data in order (usually O(n log n)); once sorted, binary search finds any item by repeatedly halving the data (O(log n)). Sorting is arranging items into order — numbers ascending, names alphabetical, orders by date. It's one of the most common operations in all of software, and how you do it matters enormously at scale. Searching is finding a particular item, and the two are deeply linked: sorting is often worth doing *because* it makes searching dramatically faster. The headline searching trick is binary search. On a sorted array, you check the middle item: too big? the answer's in the left half. Too small? the right half. Either way you discard *half* the remaining items in one comparison, so even a million items take about 20 checks. That's O(log n) — logarithmic time. The catch is non-negotiable: the data must be sorted first, or binary search gives wrong answers. Good sorting algorithms — merge sort, quicksort, heapsort — run in O(n log n) time, which is provably about the best any comparison-based sort can do. They beat the naive ‘compare every pair' sorts (bubble, insertion, selection) that run in O(n²) and become unusable on large data. The ones in your language's standard library are tuned hybrids of these fast algorithms. Sorting and searching are foundational because *ordered data is fast data*. A sorted array supports binary search, finding ranges (‘all orders between two dates'), de-duplication, and merging — none of which are practical on a jumbled pile. The reason databases build sorted indexes is precisely to convert slow full scans into fast log-time lookups. The trade-offs are about *which* algorithm. Merge sort is predictable and stable but uses extra memory; quicksort is faster on average but has rare bad cases and isn't stable; the O(n²) sorts are dead simple and genuinely fine for tiny inputs but ruinous at scale. And binary search's blistering speed always comes with the precondition that someone paid to sort the data first. Binary search — O(log n): Halve a *sorted* array each comparison. Wildly fast — but only on sorted data. Merge sort — O(n log n): Split in half, sort each half, merge them. Steady and predictable; great for huge/external data. Quicksort — O(n log n) avg: Pick a pivot, partition around it, recurse. Usually fastest in practice; rare bad cases hit O(n²). O(n²) sorts: Bubble/insertion/selection — simple and fine for tiny lists, disastrous on large ones. Linear search — O(n): Just scan every item. No sorting needed, works on anything — but slow on big data. Fine for small or one-off lookups. Hash table — O(1): If you only need ‘is this exact key present?', a hash beats binary search — but gives no order or ranges. Tree / database index: Keeps data sorted *as it changes*, so you get fast search without re-sorting after every insert.

chunks.title: Sorting & searching — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Run binary search on data that *isn't* actually sorted and it returns confidently wrong answers — no crash, just silently incorrect, which is the worst kind of bug. Ship an O(n²) sort that sailed through testing on 50 rows and watch it freeze the server on 50,000. And the off-by-one boundary errors in a hand-written binary search are so notorious that ‘I wrote a bug-free binary search first try' is a small badge of honour. Tiny lists: any sort works; even O(n²) is fine, and libraries often use a simple sort below a threshold. Large in-memory data: O(n log n) sorts and binary search are the difference between instant and frozen. Data bigger than memory: external merge sort streams it in sorted chunks from disk. Planet-scale: sorting is distributed across many machines (the ‘shuffle and sort' phase of big-data jobs), but the O(n log n) limit and the halving trick you learn here still set the rules.

chunks.title: Big-O notation
chunks.text: The language for ‘how much slower does this get as the data gets bigger?' — the single most useful idea in the whole subject. Big-O describes how an algorithm's running time (or memory) grows as the input grows, ignoring constants — so you can compare approaches before you ever run them. Big-O notation answers one question: *as the input gets bigger, how fast does the work grow?* It's not a stopwatch time in seconds — those depend on your machine, the language, the weather. It's the shape of the growth, which is what actually decides whether something survives at scale. Big-O is the shared language engineers use to argue about efficiency, and it's arguably the most important single concept in computer science. It works by ignoring the noise and keeping the trend. We drop constant factors and small terms, because for large inputs they don't matter — 2n + 5 and 100n are both just O(n) (grows in step with the input), since doubling the input roughly doubles the work either way. What matters is the *category* of growth, not the exact coefficient. The categories you'll meet, from blissful to disastrous as data grows: O(1) constant (same cost no matter the size — a hash lookup); O(log n) logarithmic (barely grows — binary search); O(n) linear (grows in step — one scan); O(n log n) (a good sort); O(n²) quadratic (grows with the *square* — nested loops, painful fast); and O(2ⁿ) exponential (effectively hopeless beyond tiny inputs — naive recursion that tries everything). Big-O exists so you can judge an algorithm before writing or running it, and so two engineers can compare approaches without arguing about hardware. It's the tool that lets you predict, on paper, that one solution will sail through a million records while another will choke at ten thousand — turning ‘it feels slow' into a precise, decidable engineering question. Its deliberate blind spot is also its power: by ignoring constants, it tells you about *scaling*, not absolute speed. So a caveat — for small inputs, a ‘worse' Big-O can actually win (a simple O(n²) sort beats a fancy O(n log n) one on ten items, because the constants and simplicity dominate). Big-O is about what happens as things *grow*; it's the right lens for scale, not always for the tiny case in front of you today. O(1) — constant: Cost doesn't change with size. The dream: hash-table lookup, array index. O(log n) — logarithmic: Grows a tiny bit as data multiplies. Binary search, balanced-tree lookup. O(n) / O(n log n): Linear: one pass. n log n: a good sort. Both scale gracefully to large data. O(n²) and O(2ⁿ): Quadratic (nested loops) hurts fast; exponential is unusable beyond tiny inputs. Red flags. Actual benchmarking: Measure real milliseconds on real hardware. Catches constants and cache effects Big-O ignores — but only for the sizes you test. Big-Θ and Big-Ω: Tighter relatives: Θ pins the exact growth, Ω the best case. Big-O (the upper bound) is the one used in everyday practice. Profiling: Find *where* real time goes in a running program. Complements Big-O: theory tells you the shape, profiling tells you the hotspot.

chunks.title: Big-O notation — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Misjudging Big-O is how ‘worked in the demo, died in production' happens: a hidden nested loop (O(n²)) is invisible on test data and lethal at scale. But over-applying it bites too — obsessing over Big-O on a list that will never exceed 20 items wastes effort and can make code needlessly complex (and even slower for that tiny size). The skill is knowing *when* growth matters, then refusing to ship the quadratic surprise. Big-O *is* the language of scale — it's the lens that tells you, before you build, whether an approach reaches from ten users to a million. At small sizes constants dominate and Big-O can mislead; as data grows it becomes the decisive factor; at planet-scale it governs not just single algorithms but whole architectures (why we shard, cache, and index — each one is an effort to beat a bad growth curve). It is the through-line from a first ‘hello world' to designing systems for billions.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Database indexes — B-trees, composite & covering
chunks.title: Database indexes — B-trees, composite & covering
chunks.text: A pre-sorted lookup structure that lets the database jump straight to the rows you want instead of reading every one. An index is a separate, sorted data structure (almost always a B+-tree) that maps column values to row locations, so a query can find matching rows in a few steps instead of scanning the whole table — at the cost of extra storage and slower writes. A table without an index is just a pile of rows. To answer 'find the user with email X', the database has no choice but to read every row and check — a full table scan. On a thousand rows that's instant; on a hundred million it's a disaster. An index is a second, pre-sorted structure built over one or more columns that lets the database jump almost directly to the matching rows, the way a book's index lets you find a topic without reading every page. The structure underneath is almost always a B-tree, or more precisely a B+-tree: a shallow, wide, balanced tree where each node holds many keys and points to child nodes, and all the actual values live in the leaf level, which is itself a linked list. Because it's wide and balanced, even a billion rows sit only three or four levels deep — so a lookup is three or four steps, not a billion. The leaves being linked is what makes range queries ('all orders between two dates') and ORDER BY cheap: you find the start and walk sideways. Two ideas turn a basic index into a powerful one. A composite index covers several columns in order — (customer_id, created_at) — and works like a phone book sorted by last name then first name: brilliant for 'this customer's orders newest-first', useless for searching by created_at alone. A covering index includes every column a query needs, so the database answers entirely from the index and never touches the table at all — the fastest read there is. Indexes are the single biggest lever on read performance. The difference between an indexed and an unindexed lookup on a large table is the difference between sub-millisecond and seconds — between a snappy app and timeouts. Almost every slow query in production traces back to a missing or mis-ordered index, and adding the right one is often a one-line fix with a hundredfold payoff. But indexes are not free, and that's the whole tension. Each one is extra storage, and — crucially — every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE must update every index on the table, so writes get slower as indexes pile up. The art is indexing exactly the columns your real queries filter and sort by, and no more: enough to make reads fast, few enough to keep writes cheap. B+-tree: A wide, balanced tree with all values in a linked leaf level. Shallow depth means any lookup is a handful of steps even on huge tables. Primary vs secondary index: The primary (often the primary key) usually dictates row storage order; secondary indexes are extra trees pointing back at rows. Composite index: An index on several columns in a fixed order. Usable left-to-right only — its leftmost-prefix rule decides which queries it can help. Covering index: An index that already holds every column a query reads, so the engine answers from the index alone — no trip to the table. Selectivity / cardinality: How many distinct values a column has. High-selectivity columns (email) make great indexes; low-selectivity ones (a boolean flag) rarely do. Other index types: Hash (exact-match only), GIN/GiST (full-text, arrays, geo), and partial indexes (only rows matching a condition) for specialized jobs. Full table scan: No index — read every row. Genuinely best when the table is tiny or the query matches most of it; catastrophic on large selective lookups. Hash index: A hash table instead of a tree: O(1) exact-match lookups, but useless for ranges or ordering. Niche; B-trees are the default for a reason. Covering / included columns: Bolt extra read-only columns onto an index so it answers a query alone. Bigger index, but skips the table fetch entirely. Materialized views / denormalization: Pre-compute the answer instead of indexing the inputs. Faster reads still, at the cost of staleness and refresh logic.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Database indexes — B-trees, composite & covering
chunks.title: Database indexes — B-trees, composite & covering — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Index every column 'just in case' and your writes crawl while half the indexes are never used, wasting storage and slowing every insert. Get composite column order backwards and the planner quietly ignores the index you were counting on. Index a low-cardinality column (a status flag with three values) and the planner skips it anyway because a scan is cheaper. Wrap an indexed column in a function (WHERE lower(email) = ?) and the index can't be used — the value it stored no longer matches. And forget that a write-heavy table pays for every index on every write, so the right number of indexes is the smallest set that makes your real queries fast. Local: a primary-key index on a small SQLite or Postgres table — every lookup is fast because there's barely any data. Production: deliberate B-tree indexes on the columns your real queries filter and sort by, a few well-ordered composite indexes, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE in your toolkit to catch the slow ones. Enterprise: index audits that drop the unused, partial and covering indexes tuned to specific hot queries, and write-path budgets that cap how many indexes a hot table may carry. Planet-scale: indexes maintained per shard across a partitioned fleet, specialized structures (GIN for search, geo indexes) alongside the B-trees, and online index builds so adding one never locks a table serving millions of requests a second.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Query optimization — the planner & EXPLAIN
chunks.title: Query optimization — the planner & EXPLAIN
chunks.text: How the database turns your SQL into a step-by-step execution plan, picks the cheapest one, and how you read it when it picks wrong. Query optimization is the database's job of translating declarative SQL into the cheapest physical execution plan — choosing scan methods, join algorithms, and join order from cost estimates built on table statistics — and EXPLAIN is the window that shows you the plan it chose. SQL is declarative: you say *what* you want ('these columns where this is true, joined to that, ordered this way'), not *how* to get it. Something has to decide the *how* — which index to use, whether to scan, in what order to join three tables, which join algorithm. That something is the query planner (or optimizer), and for a query touching several tables there can be thousands of valid ways to execute it, ranging from milliseconds to minutes. The planner picks by cost estimation. It keeps statistics about each table — row counts, how many distinct values a column has, how values are distributed — and uses them to *estimate* how many rows each step will produce and how much work it'll cost. It then chooses the plan with the lowest estimated cost. The estimate is everything: when the statistics are stale or the data is skewed, the planner guesses wrong and picks a bad plan even though the database is healthy. EXPLAIN is how you see the plan: a tree of operations the database *will* run — sequential scan, index scan, nested-loop join, hash join, sort. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and shows estimated *versus actual* row counts, which is the single most useful diagnostic in databases: a step that estimated 10 rows but produced 2 million tells you exactly where the planner was fooled, and that's almost always the root of a slow query. Without an optimizer, you'd have to hand-write the execution strategy for every query — choosing indexes and join orders manually — and rewrite it whenever the data shape changed. The planner does this automatically and re-decides as the data grows, which is the entire reason SQL can be declarative. It's one of the most sophisticated pieces of any database, and it's why the same query stays fast as a table goes from thousands to millions of rows. But the optimizer is only as good as its estimates, and that's why *you* still need to understand it. The most common production performance fire is not a missing feature — it's a query that 'suddenly' got slow because statistics went stale or data grew skewed, and the planner flipped to a bad plan. Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE, spotting the estimate that's off by orders of magnitude, and nudging the planner back on track is a core, evergreen engineering skill. Parser & rewriter: Turns SQL text into an internal tree and applies rule-based simplifications before any costing begins. Statistics: Per-column row counts, distinct values, and distribution histograms the planner uses to estimate how many rows each step yields. Cost model: A formula weighing disk reads, CPU, and memory to assign each candidate plan a number; the lowest-cost plan wins. Scan methods: Sequential scan (read all rows), index scan (use a B-tree), or index-only scan (covering index) — the ways to read a single table. Join algorithms: Nested-loop (small inputs), hash join (large unsorted inputs), merge join (already-sorted inputs) — and choosing the join order matters most of all. EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Show the chosen plan, and (ANALYZE) run it to compare estimated vs actual rows and time — the core debugging tool. Query hints / forced plans: Override the optimizer to force a specific index or join. A last resort — it fixes today's plan but ignores tomorrow's data, and rots over time. Rewriting the query: Restructure the SQL so the planner naturally picks a better plan (avoid functions on indexed columns, break up a monster query). Usually the right fix. Materialized views: Pre-compute and store an expensive result, so the planner reads a small table instead of optimizing a huge join every time. Trades freshness for speed. Caching the result: Skip the database entirely for repeated reads (see caching). Doesn't make the query faster — avoids running it at all.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Query optimization — the planner & EXPLAIN
chunks.title: Query optimization — the planner & EXPLAIN — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Let statistics go stale after a big load and the planner estimates against old row counts, choosing a plan that was right yesterday and ruinous today. Wrap an indexed column in a function or a leading wildcard LIKE '%x' and the planner silently abandons the index. Write a query that forces a bad join order on skewed data and one intermediate step explodes to billions of rows. Reach for query hints to force a plan and you freeze a decision that should adapt as data grows. The discipline: keep statistics fresh, read EXPLAIN ANALYZE for estimate-vs-actual gaps, and fix the cause rather than overriding the planner. Local: the planner trivially picks index scans on a tiny database and you rarely think about it. Production: you run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on slow endpoints, keep auto-ANALYZE healthy, and fix the occasional bad plan by adding an index or rewriting a query. Enterprise: plan regressions are monitored, slow-query logs and pg_stat_statements surface the worst offenders, statistics targets are tuned on skewed columns, and critical queries have reviewed plans. Planet-scale: distributed query planners split work across shards and regions, cost models account for network transfer, adaptive execution re-plans mid-query when estimates prove wrong, and plan stability is a tracked SLO because a single regression can topple a fleet.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Database replication — primaries, replicas & failover
chunks.title: Database replication — primaries, replicas & failover
chunks.text: Keeping live copies of your database on other machines — so reads scale out, a dead server doesn't lose data, and the system survives a failure. Replication continuously copies a database's changes from a primary to one or more replicas, so you can serve reads from the copies, survive the loss of any single machine, and promote a replica to take over when the primary fails — trading some consistency for availability and scale. A single database server is a single point of failure: if its disk dies, your data and your uptime die with it. Replication fixes this by keeping live, continuously-updated copies of the database on other machines. One node, the primary (or leader), accepts all the writes; it streams every change to one or more replicas (followers) that apply those changes to stay in sync. Now there are several copies of the truth instead of one. This buys three distinct things. Durability and failover: if the primary dies, a replica already holds the data and can be promoted to become the new primary, so you lose neither the data nor (for long) the service. Read scaling: read-only queries can be spread across the replicas, so a read-heavy app serves far more traffic than one machine could. Geographic reach: replicas in other regions put a local copy near distant users. The central tension is synchronous vs asynchronous. With async replication (the common default) the primary commits a write and tells the user 'done' *before* the replicas have it — fast, but a replica may lag behind by milliseconds to seconds, so a read from a replica can be slightly stale (replication lag), and a crash at the wrong moment can lose the last few writes. With synchronous replication the primary waits for a replica to confirm before saying 'done' — no data loss on failover, but every write is slower and a slow replica drags the whole system down. Replication is how a database stops being a single point of failure. The moment data matters, you cannot bet the business on one disk: a replica turns 'we lost the database' into 'we promoted a replica and kept running'. It's the foundation of high availability and disaster recovery, and it's table stakes for any production system handling real users or money. It's also the cheapest way to scale reads, which most apps are dominated by — adding replicas multiplies read capacity without touching the write path. The price is the consistency tax: async replicas can serve stale data, so 'read your own write' bugs appear (a user updates their profile, gets routed to a lagging replica, and sees the old value). Choosing where to read, and how much lag and potential loss you'll tolerate, becomes a real design decision. Primary (leader): The single node that accepts writes and is the source of truth all replicas copy from. Replica (follower): A node that continuously applies the primary's changes; serves reads and stands ready to be promoted. Replication log (WAL): The stream of changes the primary ships — Postgres streams its write-ahead log; MySQL ships its binlog. Sync vs async: Whether the primary waits for a replica to confirm before committing. Sync = no data loss, slower; async = fast, possible lag and loss. Failover & promotion: Detecting a dead primary and promoting a replica to replace it — automatic (with a coordinator) or manual. Replication lag: How far behind a replica is. The reason a read just after a write may not see it on a replica. Single server + backups: One node, periodic backups. Simple and cheap; a failure means downtime and losing everything since the last backup. Fine for low-stakes apps only. Synchronous replication: Primary waits for a replica before committing. Zero data loss on failover; every write is slower and a slow replica stalls the system. Multi-leader / leaderless: Several nodes accept writes for cross-region scale and partition tolerance, at the cost of write conflicts and eventual consistency the app must handle. Sharding (instead of/with): Split the data so each shard's write load is smaller (see partitioning and sharding). Solves write scale, which replication alone can't; usually combined with it.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Database replication — primaries, replicas & failover
chunks.title: Database replication — primaries, replicas & failover — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Read from an async replica right after a write and the user sees stale data — the classic 'I updated it but it didn't change' bug. Run synchronous replication with one slow replica and every write across the whole system stalls behind it. Forget that async failover loses un-shipped writes and you quietly drop the last few transactions during an outage. Run multi-leader without a conflict-resolution plan and two regions silently overwrite each other. And assuming replicas scale *writes* is the deepest trap — every replica still applies every write, so replication scales reads only; write scale needs sharding. Local: a single database, maybe one replica for practice — no real availability concern. Production: a primary with one or two async replicas, reads load-balanced across them, automatic failover via a managed service, and a few queries pinned to the primary to dodge lag. Enterprise: multiple replicas per primary, cross-region replicas for DR and locality, monitored replication lag with alerts, and tested failover runbooks with defined RTO/RPO targets. Planet-scale: globally distributed topologies — regional primaries, leaderless or multi-leader designs where writes must scale and survive partitions, quorum reads/writes, and consensus protocols underneath to keep the copies agreeing as machines and whole regions come and go.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Partitioning & sharding — splitting data to scale writes
chunks.title: Partitioning & sharding — splitting data to scale writes
chunks.text: Cutting one too-big table or database into many smaller pieces — so no single machine has to hold all the data or take all the writes. Partitioning splits a large table into smaller pieces, and sharding spreads those pieces across separate machines by a shard key — letting writes and storage scale past what one server can hold, at the cost of cross-shard queries and rebalancing complexity. Replication copies a database so reads scale and failures survive — but every replica still applies *every* write and holds *all* the data, so it can't help when the dataset or the write rate outgrows a single machine. Partitioning and sharding solve that by *splitting* the data. Partitioning divides one big table into smaller chunks (often within one database); sharding takes those chunks and puts them on *different machines*, so each server owns only a slice of the data and handles only that slice's writes. Everything hinges on the shard key — the column whose value decides which shard a row lives on (user id, tenant id, region). Two common strategies: range partitioning ('users A–M here, N–Z there', or 'this month's data on this shard') keeps related rows together and makes range scans easy, but risks hotspots if one range gets all the traffic. Hash partitioning runs the key through a hash to scatter rows evenly, which spreads load beautifully but destroys locality — a range query now has to ask every shard. Choosing the shard key is the most consequential — and least reversible — decision. A good key spreads both data and load evenly and keeps the queries you run most often inside a single shard. A bad one creates a hotspot (one celebrity user's shard melts while others idle) or forces cross-shard queries and cross-shard transactions, which are slow and complex because no single machine can answer them or guarantee atomicity alone. Re-sharding later, once data is live, is famously painful. There is a hard ceiling to one machine: a finite disk, a finite write throughput, finite memory. Replication can't lift it because every node still takes every write. Sharding is the answer when you genuinely outgrow a single server — it's the only way to scale writes and total storage horizontally, by ensuring each machine is responsible for only a fraction of both. The biggest systems on earth run on it. But sharding is a serious step up in complexity and should be a *last* resort, reached only after indexing, caching, read replicas, and a bigger box have been exhausted. It complicates every cross-shard query, makes multi-row transactions hard, demands a thoughtful shard key you can't easily change, and turns rebalancing into a project. The discipline is to delay it as long as honestly possible, then choose the shard key with great care. Shard key: The column whose value maps a row to a shard. The single most important — and hardest to change — design choice. Range partitioning: Split by contiguous key ranges or time windows. Great locality and range scans; prone to hotspots and uneven fill. Hash partitioning: Hash the key to scatter rows evenly across shards. Excellent load spread; range queries must hit every shard. Hotspot: A single shard receiving a disproportionate share of data or traffic — the failure mode a bad shard key creates. Routing layer: The logic (in the app, a proxy, or the database) that sends each query to the shard(s) holding its data. Rebalancing / re-sharding: Moving data when you add shards or a hotspot appears. Consistent hashing minimizes how much must move. Vertical scaling (bigger box): Buy more CPU/RAM/disk for one server. Far simpler; always try first. Hits a hard ceiling and gets expensive at the top end. Read replicas only: Scale reads by replication without splitting data (see database replication). Solves read load; does nothing for write or storage limits. Functional / vertical partitioning: Put different tables on different databases (users here, orders there). Easier than sharding one table; doesn't help a single huge table. NewSQL / distributed SQL: Databases (Spanner, CockroachDB, Vitess) that shard and rebalance automatically under a single SQL interface. Hides the pain at the cost of adopting a new system.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Partitioning & sharding — splitting data to scale writes
chunks.title: Partitioning & sharding — splitting data to scale writes — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Choose a shard key with low cardinality or skewed traffic and you create a hotspot — one shard melts while the rest idle, and you've gained nothing. Run queries that omit the shard key and every read becomes a slow scatter-gather across all machines. Need a transaction spanning two shards and you're forced into two-phase commit or sagas, fragile and slow. Shard with key mod N and adding one server reshuffles nearly all your data. And sharding too early — before exhausting indexes, caching, and a bigger box — buys enormous complexity to solve a problem you didn't yet have. Local: one database, no sharding — you may partition a table by date just to keep queries fast. Production: vertical scaling and read replicas carry you; you partition the biggest tables by time and prune, but everything still fits on one primary. Enterprise: a genuinely large table is sharded by a carefully chosen key across several database servers (Vitess/Citus), each shard replicated, with a routing layer keeping common queries shard-local. Planet-scale: hundreds of shards across regions, consistent hashing and virtual nodes for painless rebalancing, automatic split/merge of hot ranges, and a distributed-SQL layer presenting one logical database over a fleet that serves millions of writes per second.

chunks.title: Change data capture (CDC)
chunks.text: Streaming a database's row-level changes out as they happen, by tailing its transaction log — instead of repeatedly re-reading the whole table. Change data capture turns a database's internal transaction log into a live stream of inserts, updates, and deletes, so other systems — warehouses, caches, search indexes, microservices — stay in sync in near real time without polling or dual-writes. Data created in one place almost always needs to show up elsewhere: your app's database changes, and a warehouse, a search index, a cache, and other services all need to know. The naive fixes are bad. Polling ('every minute, re-read everything that changed') is laggy, misses deletes, and hammers the source. Dual writes ('write to the database *and* publish an event in the app code') break the moment one succeeds and the other fails, silently drifting the two systems apart. Change data capture solves this at the right layer. Every transactional database already writes a transaction log — Postgres's WAL, MySQL's binlog — recording every committed row change for its own crash recovery. CDC tails that log: it reads the stream of changes the database is already producing and emits them as a clean feed of events — 'row 42 in orders was inserted with these values', 'row 17 was updated', 'row 9 was deleted'. The source database does no extra work beyond what it already does. This is log-based CDC, the modern standard (Debezium is the dominant tool), and it's powerful because it's *complete and ordered*: it captures every change including deletes, in commit order, with before-and-after values, and it can't drift because it reads the same source of truth the database commits to. The events are typically published to Kafka, where any number of downstream consumers read them independently — making CDC the bridge between your operational database and the whole event-driven and analytics world. CDC removes the two classic failure modes of keeping systems in sync. It eliminates polling (no lag, no missed deletes, no load on the source from repeated full reads) and it eliminates dual writes (no chance of the database and the event stream disagreeing, because there's only one write — to the database — and the event is *derived* from it). One source of truth, faithfully fanned out. It also decouples producers from consumers exactly like Kafka does: the application just writes to its database as it always has, and any number of downstream systems — present or future — can subscribe to the change feed without the application changing at all. That's why CDC has become the standard way to feed warehouses, sync microservices, and bridge a monolith's database into an event-driven world. The trade is real operational weight and the discipline of idempotent, schema-tolerant consumers. Transaction log (WAL/binlog): The change record the database already writes for recovery. Log-based CDC reads this — the complete, ordered, low-overhead source. Connector / capture process: The component (e.g. Debezium) that tails the log, decodes it, and emits structured change events. Change event: A message describing one row change — operation (insert/update/delete), before/after values, table, and a position/LSN. Snapshot + stream: An initial full read of existing rows, then a switch to streaming only new changes — so consumers start with the whole table, then stay current. Offset / log position: Where the capture process has read up to (the LSN). Lets it resume exactly after a restart without missing or duplicating. Sink: The downstream that consumes the events — a warehouse, search index, cache, or another service. Polling for changes: Periodically query rows changed since last run (by an updated_at column). Simple; laggy, misses deletes, loads the source, easy to get subtly wrong. Dual writes / outbox: Write the event in app code. Naive dual-write drifts on partial failure; the transactional outbox pattern fixes it — and CDC often reads that outbox. Trigger-based CDC: Database triggers write changes to an audit table. Works without log access; adds write overhead and is harder to scale than log-based. Batch full reload: Re-copy whole tables on a schedule. Dead simple and robust; far from real time and wasteful as data grows.

chunks.title: Change data capture (CDC) — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Build non-idempotent sinks and a single connector restart double-applies changes (duplicate rows, double-counted metrics). Forget that an unconsumed replication slot keeps the source's log from being recycled and the source database's disk silently fills until it crashes. Ignore schema changes in the source and an added or dropped column breaks every downstream consumer. Assume events are globally ordered when ordering only holds per table/partition and you reassemble related changes wrong. CDC is reliable only when consumers are idempotent and schema-tolerant, and the log's growth is actually consumed and monitored. Local: a single Debezium connector tailing one Postgres database into a local Kafka, mirroring a few tables — CDC in miniature. Production: connectors capturing the key tables, publishing per-table topics to Kafka, with idempotent sinks keeping a warehouse, a search index, and a cache fresh within seconds, and replication-slot lag monitored. Enterprise: CDC across many source databases feeding a central event backbone, a schema registry enforcing change-event contracts, dead-letter handling, and CDC as the standard integration path between services and into analytics. Planet-scale: high-throughput capture from sharded, multi-region databases, exactly-once stream-processing topologies built on the change feeds, and the log stream treated as the authoritative real-time spine that warehouses, caches, indexes, and services are all rebuilt from by replay.

chunks.title: Time-series databases
chunks.text: Databases built for one shape of data — a relentless stream of timestamped measurements — and the append-mostly, time-windowed queries that go with it. A time-series database is specialized for data that is timestamped, append-only, and queried by time window — using time-based partitioning, heavy columnar compression, automatic downsampling, and retention policies to ingest millions of points per second and answer 'over the last hour/day/month' queries fast. Some data is fundamentally a stream of measurements over time: a server's CPU every second, a sensor's temperature every reading, a stock price every tick, a request's latency on every call. This data has a peculiar shape — it's almost always appended (you rarely update or delete an old reading), it arrives in a relentless high-volume firehose, and you query it by time window and aggregation ('average CPU per minute over the last 6 hours', not 'find this one row by id'). A general-purpose database can store it, but it's the wrong tool for that shape. A time-series database (TSDB) — InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus, ClickHouse for analytics — is built around exactly this shape. Its core trick is time-based partitioning: data is bucketed into time chunks, so a 'last hour' query touches one small chunk and ignores years of history, and old chunks can be dropped wholesale. Because adjacent timestamps and similar metric values compress extraordinarily well, TSDBs lean on columnar storage and specialized compression (delta-of-delta on timestamps, run-length on repeated values) to store the firehose at a tiny fraction of the raw size. Two features fall naturally out of this. Downsampling / continuous aggregates: raw per-second data is automatically rolled up into per-minute and per-hour summaries, so long-range queries read pre-computed aggregates instead of billions of raw points. Retention policies: because old detail rarely matters, the database automatically expires raw data after a window (keep raw for 7 days, hourly rollups for 2 years, then delete) — turning the otherwise-unbounded firehose into a bounded, affordable store. The volume and shape of time-series data break general-purpose databases. A relational table taking millions of inserts per second, indexed for point lookups it never gets, queried with hand-rolled time-bucketing SQL, will struggle on ingestion, balloon in storage, and run slow aggregations. A TSDB matches the workload exactly — append-optimized writes, time-partitioned reads, aggressive compression, automatic rollups and expiry — turning an impossible workload into a routine one, often at a fraction of the storage cost. And this data is everywhere modern systems care about: observability (metrics that power dashboards and alerts), IoT and sensors, finance, application and infrastructure monitoring, and product analytics. The trade-offs are that a TSDB is specialized — it's not where you put your users and orders — and that you have to design tags around cardinality and accept that old data lives only as summaries. Within its niche it's dramatically better; outside it, the wrong choice. Time-based partitioning: Data bucketed into time chunks so time-window queries scan one chunk and old chunks drop in one operation. Columnar + delta compression: Storing values by column and exploiting that timestamps and readings change little, so the firehose compresses to a fraction of raw size. Downsampling / continuous aggregates: Automatic roll-ups (per-second to per-minute to per-hour) so long-range queries read summaries, not raw points. Retention policy: Rules that auto-expire old raw data, bounding storage of an otherwise-infinite stream. Tags / labels & high cardinality: Metadata (host, region, sensor) you group and filter by. Too many distinct combinations (high cardinality) is the classic TSDB performance killer. Ingestion path: A write path tuned for huge append-only throughput — batched, append-optimized, often with an in-memory buffer before flushing to chunks. Relational table with a timestamp index: Just store points in Postgres/MySQL. Fine at low volume; struggles on ingestion, storage, and aggregation as the firehose grows. Wide-column store (Cassandra): Time-bucketed rows in a leaderless store scale writes well; you build downsampling and retention yourself rather than getting them built-in. Columnar analytics DB (ClickHouse): Blazing time-window aggregations and compression; more of a general analytics engine, less of the TSDB lifecycle automation out of the box. Metrics-native (Prometheus): Purpose-built for monitoring with pull-based scraping and PromQL. Superb for ops metrics; not a general data store and weak on long retention alone.

chunks.title: Time-series databases — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Put a high-cardinality value (user id, request id) into a tag and the series count explodes, devouring memory and indexes until the database falls over — the number-one TSDB mistake. Skip downsampling and long-range queries scan billions of raw points and time out. Forget retention and the unbounded firehose fills the disk. Use a TSDB as your primary transactional store and you'll fight its append-only, eventually-summarized model on every update. And running time-series load on a general relational database without time-partitioning means ingestion chokes and aggregations crawl. The fit is narrow but, inside it, decisive. Local: a single TimescaleDB or InfluxDB instance ingesting one app's metrics, with a basic retention policy — time-series in miniature. Production: a TSDB behind your observability stack taking thousands of points per second, continuous aggregates powering dashboards, retention tiering raw-to-rollup, and tags kept deliberately low-cardinality. Enterprise: a clustered TSDB ingesting millions of points per second across many services and sensor fleets, multi-tier downsampling, long-term cold storage for compliance, and cardinality budgets enforced per team. Planet-scale: globally distributed ingestion with regional write paths, sharded by series and time, automatic compaction and tiered storage to object stores, and the time-series layer feeding both real-time alerting and long-horizon trend analysis over trillions of points.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — How a CPU works
chunks.title: How a CPU works
chunks.text: What 'running code' physically is: a tiny machine fetching numbers and doing one of them, billions of times a second. A CPU is a machine that endlessly repeats one loop — fetch the next instruction, figure out what it means, do it — driven by a clock that ticks billions of times a second. Underneath every program is a CPU (the processor): a fingernail-sized slab of silicon whose entire job is to run one loop, forever, called fetch-decode-execute. Fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it, then move on. That loop *is* what people mean when they say a computer is 'running' your code. The instructions it runs are machine code — bare numbers like 'add slot A to slot B', 'compare these two', 'jump to instruction #4096'. Your cartTotal += price becomes a handful of those. The CPU has no idea it's adding up a burger order; it only sees numbers and operations. The CPU works on a tiny handful of ultra-fast scratch slots called registers — not the big wall of RAM, but a dozen-odd named slots right inside the chip. To add two numbers, it loads them into registers, the ALU (the arithmetic unit) adds them, and the result goes back into a register, maybe later to memory. Everything is paced by a clock that ticks billions of times a second; each tick lets the next bit of work happen. Why build computing on something this primitive? Because a machine that does only the simplest possible things — but does them billions of times a second, perfectly, forever — turns out to be enough to build everything. The fetch-decode-execute loop is dumb on purpose: its simplicity is what makes it fast, cheap, and utterly reliable. All the apparent intelligence lives in the *arrangement* of those tiny instructions, not in any one of them. Understanding the loop demystifies a lot. Why is reading from disk a disaster for speed while reading a register is free? Because one is the filing cabinet across the room and the other is the sticky note in front of you. Why did programs suddenly need to be written to use many cores? Because the metronome stopped speeding up and they gave you more workers instead. Fetch-decode-execute: The eternal loop: read the next instruction, work out what it is, carry it out, repeat. This loop is 'running'. Registers: A dozen-odd ultra-fast slots inside the CPU it actually computes on. Far faster than RAM, but tiny. ALU: Arithmetic & Logic Unit — the part that adds, subtracts, compares, and does AND/OR. The 'doing' in execute. Program counter: A register holding the address of the next instruction. Normally steps forward; a 'jump' rewrites it. Clock: A signal ticking billions of times a second (GHz). Each tick paces the work — more ticks, more instructions. GPU: Thousands of simple cores doing the same operation on lots of data at once — slow for branchy logic, brilliant for graphics and ML matrix math. ASIC / TPU: A chip hard-wired for one job (Bitcoin hashing, neural-net math). Fastest and most efficient possible, but can do only that one thing. FPGA: Reconfigurable hardware — you 'wire up' a custom circuit in software. A middle ground between a flexible CPU and a fixed ASIC. Quantum processor: A different model of computation entirely; promising for a few specific problems, not a faster general-purpose CPU.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — How a CPU works
chunks.title: How a CPU works — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Assume the CPU is the bottleneck and you'll optimise the wrong thing. Most slow programs aren't doing too much arithmetic — they're *waiting*: on memory the cache missed, on a disk read, on a network call, on a lock another thread holds. A loop that touches memory in a cache-friendly order can be ten times faster than the same loop touching it randomly, with the exact same instruction count. The lesson: speed is usually about what the chip is stalled waiting for, not how clever your code looks. On a microcontroller in a thermostat, one slow core runs one loop and that's the whole computer. On your laptop, a handful of cores with deep caches juggle hundreds of threads. In a data center, racks of many-core machines plus GPUs and custom accelerators (TPUs) chew through training runs and millions of requests. At planet scale the single CPU stops being the unit you reason about at all — you reason about fleets of machines and the network between them — but every one of those machines is still, at bottom, running this same little loop.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Binary & how numbers are stored
chunks.title: Binary & how numbers are stored
chunks.text: Everything in a computer is a number, every number is a pattern of on/off switches — and that's why 0.1 + 0.2 isn't quite 0.3. Computers store everything as patterns of bits (on/off switches); how those bits are interpreted decides whether a pattern means 42, negative-7, the letter A, or a price that's slightly wrong. At the bottom, a computer can only hold one kind of thing: a bit — a single switch that's either off (0) or on (1). Eight of them make a byte, and a byte can hold 256 different patterns (2^8). Stack bytes together and you can represent any number, any letter, any pixel. The bits never change meaning by themselves; *the code decides* what a pattern stands for. Plain whole numbers are stored in binary — base-2, the same idea as our base-10 but with only two digits. Where we have ones, tens, hundreds, binary has ones, twos, fours, eights. So 1011 is 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. A fixed number of bits means a fixed range: 8 bits count to 255, 32 bits to about 4 billion. Go past the top and the number silently wraps around to zero — overflow. Negative numbers use a clever trick called two's complement, and fractions use floating point — and floating point is why 0.1 + 0.2 famously comes out as 0.30000000000000004. The decimal 0.1 simply has no exact representation in binary, the same way 1/3 has no exact decimal. The computer stores the closest it can, and the tiny errors add up. Why force everything down to two states? Because two states are *robust*. A switch that only has to tell 'clearly on' from 'clearly off' tolerates noise, voltage drift, and manufacturing slop far better than one trying to hold ten distinct levels. Binary is the representation that's reliable enough to build billions of switches on a chip and have them all agree. Everything else — numbers, text, images, sound — is a convention layered on top of those two states. Why tolerate floating-point imprecision at all? Because the alternative — exact representation of every possible fraction — would be impossibly large or slow for general use. Floating point is a deliberate trade: a vast range and fast hardware, in exchange for tiny, well-understood rounding errors. Knowing the trade exists is what separates 'my totals are mysteriously off by a cent' bafflement from 'right, I should be using integer cents here'. Bit: One on/off switch — 0 or 1. The smallest unit of information there is. Byte: Eight bits grouped together; holds one of 256 patterns. The basic unit memory is measured in. Binary (base-2): Counting with only two digits, place values doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… 1011 = 11. Two's complement: The standard trick for storing negative whole numbers so that ordinary addition just works. Floating point: How fractions are stored: a sign, some digits, and an exponent — like scientific notation in binary. Approximate by nature. Integer cents / minor units: Store money as a whole number of the smallest unit (cents). Exact, fast, no rounding — the standard for currency. Arbitrary-precision decimal: A type that stores decimals exactly (Java BigDecimal, Python Decimal). Slower and heavier, but no surprises — used in finance. Fixed-point: Whole numbers with an implied decimal place. Exact within its range; common in embedded and graphics work. Bignum integers: Whole numbers that grow as large as needed (Python's default ints). No overflow, at some speed and memory cost.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Binary & how numbers are stored
chunks.title: Binary & how numbers are stored — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Store a price as a floating-point number and run a few thousand orders through it, and your books drift by cents that don't reconcile — auditors hate this and the bug is invisible until totals are compared. Use a 32-bit counter for something that grows without bound and one day it wraps to a negative number, breaking every comparison that assumed it only goes up. The fixes are boring and crucial: integer cents for money, comparisons with tolerance for floats, and integer widths chosen with the maximum value in mind. In a one-off script, a float total is harmless. In a real store, integer cents become mandatory the moment money is summed across many orders. At enterprise scale, the *type and width* of a number is a design decision with consequences — a chosen integer width determines when a system overflows (the 2038 problem is exactly this), and a chosen money type determines whether the ledger ever reconciles. At planet scale, multiply one rounding error by billions of transactions and it's a line item; this is why payment systems are religious about exact decimal arithmetic.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Character encoding: ASCII, Unicode, UTF-8
chunks.title: Character encoding: ASCII, Unicode, UTF-8
chunks.text: Text is just numbers wearing a costume — and when two programs disagree on the costume, you get '□' and 'café' turning into 'cafÃ©'. A computer stores text as numbers; an encoding is the agreed table that says which number means which character — and mojibake is what you see when the writer and the reader used different tables. A computer has no idea what a letter is — it only stores numbers (which are only bits). Character encoding is the shared rulebook that says 'the number 65 means capital A, 97 means lowercase a'. Save text with one rulebook and read it with another, and every character comes out wrong. The famous garbled '?????' or 'cafÃ©' has a name: mojibake. The first widely-agreed table was ASCII — 128 characters covering English letters, digits, and punctuation, each fitting in 7 bits. That was fine for 1960s American English and hopeless for the rest of the planet: no é, no ñ, no Arabic, no Chinese, no emoji. Unicode fixed the ambition: one giant table giving every character in every human language (and emoji) a unique number called a code point — over a million slots. But Unicode only assigns the numbers; it doesn't say how to store them as bytes. That's the job of an encoding, and the one that won the web is UTF-8.
