Why not just one fixed-width encoding for everything? Because the trade-offs pull apart. A fixed 4 bytes per character (UTF-32) is simple to index but quadruples the size of English text. UTF-8 chose to be variable-width so the world's huge existing pile of ASCII stays valid and compact, while still reaching every character — paying for it with the complexity that 'one character ≠ one byte'. That single design choice is why UTF-8 is now the default of the web and why most encoding bugs are about someone forgetting it. Getting this right is the difference between software that works for *everyone* and software that works for English speakers. Names, addresses, messages, search — all of it breaks in the same ugly way the moment an encoding mismatch sneaks in, and the breakage often only shows up for users whose language you didn't test in. Encoding is unglamorous and absolutely load-bearing for anything global. Character: What a human sees: A, é, あ, an emoji. Not a number until the computer assigns one. ASCII: The original 128-character table (English letters, digits, punctuation), each in 7 bits. Still the base of everything. Code point: Unicode's unique number for one character, e.g. U+0041 for A, U+1F354 for the burger emoji. Encoding (UTF-8): The rule turning code points into actual bytes. UTF-8 uses 1–4 bytes per character and is ASCII-compatible. Grapheme: What a person counts as 'one character' — which may be several code points glued together (e.g. an emoji with a skin tone). UTF-16: 2 or 4 bytes per character; used internally by Java, JavaScript, and Windows. Compact for Asian scripts, wasteful for ASCII, and has fiddly 'surrogate pairs'. UTF-32: A flat 4 bytes per character. Trivial to index, but four times the size of ASCII text — rarely used for storage. Latin-1 / Windows-1252: Old single-byte encodings covering Western European characters. The usual culprit when UTF-8 text turns to mojibake. ASCII: The 7-bit original. Still perfect when you truly only need English letters, digits, and punctuation — and it's a strict subset of UTF-8.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Character encoding: ASCII, Unicode, UTF-8
chunks.title: Character encoding: ASCII, Unicode, UTF-8 — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: A user named 'José' signs up; somewhere in the chain a column or header is set to Latin-1 instead of UTF-8, and his name is stored or shown as 'JosÃ©'. Worse, a string is truncated at a fixed byte count for a database limit and the cut lands in the middle of a multi-byte character, producing an invalid sequence that crashes the next thing to read it. The cure is unglamorous discipline: declare UTF-8 everywhere, measure lengths in characters or graphemes (not bytes) when a human cares, and normalise before comparing. In a personal English-only script, you may never notice encoding at all — ASCII just works. The moment real users with real names arrive, end-to-end UTF-8 becomes non-negotiable. In a large product, encoding correctness is a tested, audited property of every input boundary — forms, file uploads, third-party APIs. At planet scale (a global social network, a search engine) text handling expands into full internationalisation: Unicode normalisation, locale-aware sorting and casing, right-to-left scripts, and emoji that combine into one glyph — all of it resting on getting the encoding right first.

chunks.title: Type systems
chunks.text: The rules about what kind of thing each value is — and when the language checks them: at your desk, or in front of a customer. A type system is the language's rulebook for what kind of value each thing holds and what you're allowed to do with it; the big choices are when it checks (compile-time vs run-time) and how strictly it refuses nonsense. Every value in a program has a type — a number, some text, a true/false, a list, an Order. A type system is the set of rules the language enforces about those types: you can multiply two numbers but not a number and a sentence; you can call .length on a list but not on a number. The type is a promise about what a value *is* and what it can *do*. The first big split is *when* those rules are checked. A static type system checks them ahead of time, when the code is compiled, before it ever runs — TypeScript and Dart do this. A dynamic type system checks them as the program runs, the moment a line executes — JavaScript and Python do this. Static catches whole classes of mistakes at your desk; dynamic catches them only if that exact line happens to run, possibly in production. The second split is *how strict* the language is about mixing types. A strong type system refuses to silently treat one type as another ("5" + 5 is an error); a weak one quietly coerces them (JavaScript turns "5" + 5 into "55", which surprises everyone eventually). And type inference lets a static language figure out the type for you, so you get the safety without writing the type on every line. The whole subject is one trade-off restated: safety and clarity vs flexibility and speed-of-writing. Static, strong typing catches mistakes early, documents intent (the types *are* documentation), and makes large codebases and tooling (autocomplete, safe rename) possible — at the cost of more upfront writing and a build step that can reject your code. Dynamic, weak typing is fast and loose to write and great for quick scripts — at the cost of bugs that hide until runtime. Neither is 'right'; they fit different jobs. Knowing where a language sits explains its character. Why does your TypeScript backend catch a mistake before it deploys while a plain-JavaScript one might crash live? Static vs dynamic. Why does "5" + 5 give 55 in one language and an error in another? Weak vs strong. Why do big teams keep adding types to dynamic languages? Because at scale, the cost of bugs-found-late dwarfs the cost of writing types. Static vs dynamic: When types are checked: before running (static, at compile) or while running (dynamic, as each line executes). Strong vs weak: How willingly the language coerces types. Strong refuses surprising mixes; weak silently converts ("5" + 5). Type inference: The compiler deducing a value's type so you don't have to write it — static safety, less typing. Nullability: Whether 'no value' (null) is a type the system tracks. Modern languages make null explicit to kill the billion-dollar bug. Generics: Types with a blank to fill in — a List<T> works for any element type while still being checked. Reuse without losing safety. Static + strong (Dart, Rust, Java): Checked before running, refuses surprising coercions. Catches the most at your desk; most ceremony and a build gate. Dynamic + strong (Python, Ruby): Checked at runtime, but won't silently coerce — "5" + 5 errors. Flexible to write; type bugs still surface only when the line runs. Dynamic + weak (JavaScript): Checked at runtime and coerces freely. Fast to start, famous for surprising results — which is why TypeScript exists. Gradual typing (TypeScript, Python hints): Add static checks on top of a dynamic language, file by file. Buy back safety without a full rewrite.

chunks.title: Type systems — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Lean entirely on a dynamic, weak system in a growing codebase and a refactor becomes terror: rename a field and you won't know what you broke until each path runs, and a stray coercion turns a number into a string that quietly corrupts a total. Over-index on a rigid static system and you can drown simple scripts in type ceremony, or fight the checker over code you know is fine. The skill is matching the strictness to the stakes — and reaching for gradual typing when a loose codebase has outgrown its looseness. For a ten-line script, dynamic and untyped is genuinely fine — types would just slow you down. As a codebase and team grow, static types become the load-bearing structure: they're how dozens of people change shared code without breaking each other, and how editors offer safe rename and autocomplete across millions of lines. At enterprise scale, types extend beyond one program into *contracts between systems* — typed API schemas, generated clients, validated database models — so that services written by different teams in different languages still agree on the shape of the data they exchange.

chunks.title: Garbage collection
chunks.text: The automatic janitor that frees the memory your program forgot about — and the reason an app occasionally stutters for no visible reason. Garbage collection is the language automatically reclaiming heap memory that nothing in your program can reach anymore, so you don't have to free it by hand — trading a little runtime overhead and the odd pause for freedom from a whole category of bugs. Programs constantly ask for memory on the heap to hold things that must outlive the function that made them — a growing list, a loaded image, an Order object. Someone has to give that memory back when it's no longer needed, or the program slowly eats all available RAM (a memory leak). Garbage collection (GC) is the language doing that giving-back automatically. The key idea is reachability. If no variable, no field, nothing your code could ever touch still points to a piece of heap data, then your program can never use it again — it's garbage, and its memory can be safely reclaimed. A garbage collector's job is to find that unreachable data and free it, while you go on writing code as if memory were infinite. Languages like Java, Python, Dart, JavaScript, and Go are garbage-collected — you almost never free anything by hand. The convenience is enormous, but it isn't free: the collector runs *during* your program, costs some CPU and memory, and in older designs would occasionally pause everything to do its work — the mysterious hitch in an app that's otherwise idle. Why hand this to the runtime at all? Because manual memory management is the source of some of the most dangerous, hardest-to-find bugs in software: leaks (forgot to free — the program bloats and dies), use-after-free and double-free (freed too early or twice — corruption and security holes). Garbage collection makes whole categories of those bugs simply impossible, which is a colossal gain in safety and developer speed. For the vast majority of software, that's the right trade. The trade-off is control and predictability vs safety and convenience. GC costs CPU and some extra memory headroom, and introduces pauses you don't fully control — unacceptable in a few domains (hard real-time systems, a pacemaker, the tightest game loops, an operating-system kernel) where a stutter at the wrong instant is a failure. That's why systems languages offer alternatives, and why a third path — Rust's compile-time ownership — exists: the compiler frees memory for you with neither a collector nor a pause. Reachability: The core test: can your running program still get to this data through some chain of references? If not, it's garbage. Reference counting: Each object tracks how many things point at it; hits zero, freed immediately. Simple, prompt — but can't free reference cycles. Mark-and-sweep: Periodically trace everything reachable from the 'roots' (mark), then free everything not marked (sweep). Handles cycles. Generational GC: Most objects die young, so collect new objects often and old ones rarely. The trick that makes modern GC fast. Stop-the-world pause: A moment the collector freezes the program to work safely. Modern GCs shrink these to be barely noticeable. Manual management (C, C++): You allocate and free by hand. Total control and no pauses; leaks, use-after-free, and double-free are yours to cause. Ownership / borrow checker (Rust): The compiler proves at build time exactly when to free — no garbage collector, no pauses, no leaks, at the cost of a stricter language. Reference counting (Swift, Python): Free promptly when the count hits zero. Predictable timing; needs an extra trick (or programmer care) for reference cycles. Arena / pool allocation: Allocate many objects in one block and free the whole block at once. Blazing fast for short-lived batches; not general-purpose.

chunks.title: Garbage collection — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Hold one reference you forgot about — a cache that never evicts, a listener never unregistered, a growing global list — and the collector dutifully keeps that memory *alive* forever: a leak even in a garbage-collected language, because the data is still technically reachable. Or build a latency-sensitive service that allocates churningly, and a stop-the-world pause lands mid-request, spiking your tail latency for reasons that don't show up in the code. The cure is understanding reachability (drop references you're done with) and, when latency matters, choosing or tuning a collector that keeps pauses tiny. In a short-lived script, GC is invisible — the program exits before it matters. In a long-running server, GC behaviour becomes a real engineering surface: you size the heap, pick a low-pause collector, and watch for leaks that only manifest after days of uptime. At planet scale, GC pauses show up in tail latency (the slowest 1% of requests) across millions of calls, so big services obsess over pause-free collectors, off-heap storage, and allocation patterns — and a few extreme domains abandon GC entirely for manual or ownership-based memory to get guarantees a collector can't give.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Discrete math for programmers
chunks.title: Discrete math for programmers
chunks.text: The math that's actually under the code: counting, logic, sets, and clock arithmetic — not the calculus you were told you'd need. Discrete math is the mathematics of distinct, separate things — sets, logic, counting, and modular arithmetic — and it's the quiet machinery under data structures, algorithms, and almost every correctness argument in software. Most programmers brace for calculus and never use it; the math software actually runs on is discrete — about separate, countable things rather than smooth continuous curves. Its four workhorses are sets (collections of distinct items), logic (true/false reasoning), combinatorics (counting how many arrangements exist), and modular arithmetic (wrap-around 'clock' math). You're using all four already, probably without naming them. Sets are the idea behind a database JOIN, a Set data structure that ignores duplicates, and 'show me users in A but not B'. Logic is the &&, ||, ! in every if, and the rules (like De Morgan's laws) that let you simplify a tangled condition without changing what it means. Combinatorics answers 'how many possible passwords / orders / combinations are there?' — which is the same question as 'is this search feasible or astronomically huge?'. Modular arithmetic is clock math: 10 o'clock plus 5 hours is 3, not 15, because the clock wraps at 12. Computers wrap constantly — a hash mapping any key into a fixed number of buckets, an array index cycling round a ring buffer, a fixed-width integer overflowing. Knowing this is *arithmetic with a wrap* rather than mysterious behaviour explains a surprising amount of code. Why bother naming the math you're already half-doing? Because precise names let you reason *carefully* about correctness instead of testing-and-hoping. A condition you simplify by gut might change meaning; one you simplify by De Morgan's law provably doesn't. A search you 'feel' is fine might be astronomically huge; combinatorics tells you for sure. This is the difference between code that happens to pass your tests and code you can argue is right. It's also the shared language under the rest of computer science. Data structures are built from sets and graphs; algorithm analysis is combinatorics; correctness proofs are logic and induction; hashing and cryptography are modular arithmetic. Learning the math once pays off across every one of them — and it's why CS degrees teach discrete math before, not after, the algorithms that depend on it. Sets: Collections of distinct items, with union, intersection, difference. The idea under JOINs, Set types, and de-duplication. Logic: Reasoning with true/false: AND, OR, NOT, implication, and laws to simplify conditions (De Morgan) without changing meaning. Combinatorics: Counting arrangements and choices. Tells you how big a space is — and therefore whether brute force is feasible. Modular arithmetic: Wrap-around math (clock math). Under hashing, ring buffers, checksums, and integer overflow. Graphs & relations: How discrete things connect — friendships, dependencies, routes. The bridge from this math into graph algorithms. Continuous math (calculus): For smoothly changing quantities — physics, signals, optimisation, the gradients behind ML. Useful, but not what most everyday code runs on. Linear algebra: Vectors and matrices — the math of graphics, simulations, and machine learning. A different toolkit for a different set of problems. Statistics: Drawing conclusions from data. Overlaps with probability; the go-to when you're measuring and inferring rather than counting exactly. Numerical methods: Approximating continuous math on a discrete computer (and managing the floating-point error that creeps in). Where discrete and continuous meet.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Discrete math for programmers
chunks.title: Discrete math for programmers — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Skip it and you reason about logic and counting by feel — which works until it doesn't. You negate a compound condition wrong and ship a security check that's inverted; you brute-force a problem whose space is 2^n and your job runs until the heat death of the universe; you treat hashing or overflow as black magic instead of modular arithmetic and can't predict or debug it. The failure isn't a crash so much as a quiet wrongness or an impossible-to-finish computation that careful counting would have caught on paper. On a small program, discrete-math instincts keep your conditions correct and your data operations clean. As systems grow, set thinking is what makes complex database queries and access rules tractable, and combinatorial feasibility analysis is what stops you from designing an algorithm that can't possibly finish. At planet scale, this math underpins the consistency rules of distributed systems, the modular arithmetic in cryptography that secures every connection, and the counting arguments behind capacity planning — the same handful of ideas, now load-bearing for billions of operations.

chunks.title: Probability for programmers
chunks.text: Reasoning about uncertainty and chance — the quiet math behind hashing, load balancing, retries, caches, and machine learning. Probability is the math of uncertainty — how likely outcomes are and what to expect on average — and it shows up the moment your system is big enough that 'usually' and 'on average' matter more than any single case. Probability measures how likely something is, on a scale from 0 (never) to 1 (certain). Closely tied to it is expected value — the long-run average outcome, weighted by how likely each outcome is. These two ideas let you reason about systems where you can't predict any single event but *can* predict the aggregate: not 'will this request be slow' but 'what fraction of requests will be slow, and how slow at the worst'. Programmers meet probability everywhere, often disguised. A hash table stays fast only because keys spread *roughly evenly* across buckets — a probabilistic claim. A load balancer spreads requests so no server is *usually* overwhelmed. Retries with random backoff sprinkle randomness on purpose so a thousand clients don't all retry in lockstep. Caches, sampling in monitoring, A/B tests, and all of machine learning are soaked in probability. The crucial mental shift is from worst-case to *distribution*. A single coin flip is unpredictable, but ten thousand flips land very close to 50/50 — that's the law of large numbers, and it's why systems that look chaotic up close are predictable in bulk. The flip side is the rare-but-real tail: at huge scale, one-in-a-million events happen many times a day, which is why big systems must design for the unlikely. Why does a coder need probability? Because past a certain scale, the right questions stop being deterministic. 'Will it work' becomes 'how often will it fail, and how badly in the worst 1%'. Capacity, timeouts, retries, cache sizes, and reliability targets are all *expected-value* and *distribution* decisions — you literally cannot set a sensible timeout or SLA without thinking probabilistically. The systems that stay up are designed by people who reasoned about the tail; the ones that fall over on launch day were designed for the average. It also keeps you honest. Human intuition about chance is famously bad — we underestimate collisions, overestimate independence, and fixate on averages. Knowing a little probability is a guard against expensive, confident mistakes: over-provisioning for a case that never happens, or being blindsided by a 'one-in-a-million' event that, at a million requests a minute, happens every minute. Probability: How likely an outcome is, from 0 to 1. The basic unit of reasoning about uncertainty. Expected value: The long-run average outcome, each possibility weighted by its probability. What you plan around. Independence: Whether one event affects another. Wrongly assuming independence is the source of many real-world disasters. Distributions: The full shape of how outcomes spread — not just the average, but how often the extremes happen. Tail / percentiles: The rare, slow, or extreme cases (p99, p999). At scale, the tail is where the pain lives, and where averages mislead. Statistics: The companion discipline: probability reasons forward from a model; statistics reasons backward from data to infer the model. You usually need both. Worst-case analysis: Reason about the absolute worst outcome, ignoring likelihood. Essential for safety-critical and security work, where 'rare' isn't good enough. Queueing theory: Probability specialised to waiting lines and load — the math behind 'how many servers do I need and how long will requests wait'. Simulation (Monte Carlo): When the math is too hard, run the random process thousands of times and measure. Brute-forcing probability with a computer.

chunks.title: Probability for programmers — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Reason only about the average and you'll be ambushed by the tail: an app that's 'fast on average' feels broken because a page fires 50 calls and almost always trips the slow 1%. Assume independence that isn't there and your 'redundant' systems fail together in the one correlated way you didn't model. Underestimate collisions (the birthday paradox) and your 'unique' short IDs start clashing far sooner than you swore they could. The damage is rarely a clean crash — it's a system that works in testing and small scale, then misbehaves exactly when it gets big, in ways that look like bad luck but were predictable all along. For a small program with a handful of users, probability barely registers — averages are fine and rare events almost never occur. As traffic grows, the tail starts to bite and percentile thinking becomes essential to keep the experience good. At planet scale, probability is everywhere at once: one-in-a-billion events happen constantly, so systems are engineered against the tail; load balancing, sharding, caching, and reliability targets are all probabilistic designs; and capacity planning is pure expected-value math across billions of events. The bigger the system, the more it is *governed* by probability rather than occasionally touched by it.

chunks.title: Mobile navigation
chunks.text: How screens stack, swap, and link together — the invisible map a user walks through your app. Mobile navigation is the system that decides which screen is showing, what ‘back' does, and how a tap (or a link from outside) moves the user from one screen to the next. An app isn't one screen — it's dozens, and the user is always *somewhere* in them. Navigation is the machinery that tracks where they are and moves them around: tap a burger and the detail screen slides in over the menu; press back and it slides away again. The thing being tracked is a stack — a pile of screens where the top one is what you see, and ‘back' pops the top off. There are a few distinct movements, and good apps mix them. A stack push/pop is the forward-and-back drill-down (menu → product → checkout). Tabs are parallel sections you flip between without losing your place in each (Home / Orders / Profile, each with its own little stack). A modal slides up over everything for a focused task (login, a filter sheet) and is dismissed rather than navigated past. Finally, navigation has an *outside* entrance: a deep link is a URL like burgerfarm://order/8f3 (or an https:// App/Universal Link) that opens the app *directly on a specific screen* — from a notification, a shared message, or a search result — instead of always dumping the user on the home page. Navigation is one of the first things to rot in an app. Wire screens together ad-hoc — each one pushing the next by hand — and within months ‘back' behaves differently in five places, deep links open the wrong screen, and nobody can answer ‘how does a user get here?'. A single, declarative route table makes the whole map readable in one file and the back-behaviour consistent by construction. It also unlocks things users now expect: a notification that opens the exact order, a shared link that opens the exact product, tabs that remember their place. Those are all just ‘the OS hands us a URL, the router renders the screen' — trivial with a real navigation system, near-impossible to bolt on later. The navigation stack: The pile of screens; the top is visible, push adds one, pop (or back) removes it. The user's history lives here. Routes & a router: Named destinations (/product/:id) and the code that maps a name to the screen that should appear. Tabs / nested navigators: Parallel sections, each keeping its own independent stack so switching tabs never loses your place. Deep links & link handling: URLs that open the app on a precise screen from outside — notifications, the web, another app. Passing & guarding: Carrying data into a screen (which product) and blocking routes behind auth (can't open checkout logged out). Imperative navigation: Each screen calls push(NextScreen()) directly. Dead simple for a 3-screen app; becomes an untraceable tangle with no central map as screens multiply. Declarative / URL router: A central route table maps URLs to screens (go_router, React Navigation). The modern default — deep-linkable, guardable, restorable. Single-screen + conditional UI: One screen that swaps its body based on state. Fine for a wizard or onboarding; no real back stack or deep links. Native per-platform navigation: Use each OS's own navigator (UINavigationController, Jetpack Navigation). Best platform feel; two systems to keep in sync in a cross-platform app.

chunks.title: Mobile navigation — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Push screens imperatively all over the app and ‘back' becomes a lottery — sometimes it pops one screen, sometimes it exits to home, sometimes it loops. Forget state restoration and the OS killing a backgrounded app dumps the user back on the home page mid-checkout, work lost. Let a deep link skip the auth guard and a crafted URL opens a screen the user shouldn't reach. Hold heavy screens in the stack forever and memory balloons. A single declarative route table with guards and restoration prevents all four. Local: a handful of screens pushed and popped on one stack — you can hold the whole map in your head. Production: a declarative router with named routes, parameters, tabbed sections, auth guards, and deep links from notifications and shared URLs, restored correctly after the OS reclaims the app. Enterprise: a navigation framework owned by a platform team, with feature modules registering their own routes, a versioned deep-link scheme, and A/B-testable flows so product teams reroute users without touching core code. Planet-scale: deferred/lazy-loaded feature routes (the app downloads a feature module on demand), server-driven navigation where the backend decides the next screen for personalisation and experiments, and a deep-link layer that resolves the same https:// link to web or app across dozens of locales and app versions.

chunks.title: Mobile animations
chunks.text: Motion that feels native — every frame on time, every gesture answered, nothing janky. Mobile animation is the craft of changing the screen smoothly over time inside a strict per-frame budget, so transitions and gestures feel instant and physical rather than choppy. A screen doesn't really *move* — it's redrawn many times a second, each frame slightly different, and your eye stitches the sequence into motion. Phones target 60fps (often 120fps now), which means a new frame roughly every 16 milliseconds. That 16ms is a hard frame budget: if the work for one frame takes longer, the phone misses the deadline, the frame is dropped, and the user sees a stutter — jank. So animation is really a *budgeting* discipline. Cheap things to animate are transforms — moving, scaling, rotating, fading — because they don't force the screen to recompute layout; they just re-place pixels the GPU already has. Expensive things — re-measuring layout, re-rasterising images, rebuilding big chunks of UI — eat the budget and cause drops. Native-feeling motion is mostly: animate the cheap properties, never the expensive ones, every frame. The second half is gestures. A native-feeling animation is *interruptible and tied to your finger*: a sheet you drag follows your thumb exactly, and if you fling it, it continues with physics (spring, friction, momentum) rather than snapping. The motion isn't a fixed canned clip — it's driven by your input in real time, which is what separates ‘premium' from ‘a website in an app'. Smoothness is perceived as *quality and speed* even when nothing is actually faster. A janky transition makes an app feel cheap and broken; the same screens with buttery, interruptible motion feel premium and responsive. For an app whose personality lives in motion — a radial burger builder, an animated cart — this is the difference between ‘a real product' and ‘a prototype'. It's also where ‘cross-platform' is won or lost. Because Flutter draws its own pixels, it can hit a consistent 60/120fps with custom motion on both phones — but only if you respect the frame budget. Get it right and the app feels native everywhere; get it wrong and the jank is the first thing a user notices. The frame budget (16ms): At 60fps you have ~16ms per frame to do everything. Blow it and the frame drops — visible jank. Transforms vs layout: Move/scale/rotate/fade are cheap (GPU re-places pixels); re-measuring layout each frame is expensive. Tweens & curves: Interpolating a value over a duration along an easing curve — ease-out, ease-in-out — so motion accelerates naturally. Spring / physics animation: Motion driven by stiffness, damping, and velocity rather than a fixed duration — feels physical and continues a fling. Gesture-driven & interruptible: The animation tracks the finger in real time and can be grabbed mid-flight, the hallmark of native feel. Implicit / tween animations: Declare ‘animate this property over 300ms' and the framework interpolates it. Easiest; perfect for simple state-driven transitions. Explicit controller-driven: You own an AnimationController and drive multiple values from it — needed for orchestrated, multi-part, or interruptible motion. Physics / spring: Motion from a simulation (stiffness/damping/velocity). The native-feel default for gestures and anything a user can fling. Lottie / pre-rendered: Play a designer-authored vector animation (e.g. a loading burger). Gorgeous and cheap to play, but not interactive or gesture-driven.

chunks.title: Mobile animations — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Animate layout-affecting properties every frame and the relayout cost blows the 16ms budget — visible stutter. Run a canned, non-interruptible animation and a user who grabs it mid-flight feels the app fight them. Do image decoding or JSON parsing on the UI thread during a transition and frames drop exactly when motion should be smoothest. Forget to dispose an AnimationController and you leak it, ticking forever. Respect the budget — cheap properties, springs over durations, heavy work off-thread, controllers disposed — and motion stays glassy. Local: a couple of tween animations on one screen, eyeballed as ‘smooth enough' on your dev phone. Production: a consistent motion language (shared curves, durations, reusable animated widgets), gesture-driven interruptible transitions, and profiling on real low-end devices — not just the flagship on your desk. Enterprise: a motion design system owned across teams, animations driven by a shared engine, automated performance budgets in CI that fail a build if a screen regresses on frame time, and tested across a matrix of device tiers. Planet-scale: per-device-tier motion (rich on flagships, reduced on budget phones and on ‘reduce motion' accessibility settings), 120fps where the panel allows, GPU-shader-driven effects, and frame-timing telemetry streamed from millions of real devices to catch jank regressions in the field.

chunks.title: App performance
chunks.text: Fast on the phone in someone's pocket — quick to start, smooth to use, and easy on memory and battery. App performance is making the app start fast, scroll without jank, use memory and battery sparingly, and stay responsive on a real low-end device, not just your dev phone. ‘Fast' on a phone is four different things, and they trade off against each other. Startup time is how long from tap-icon to usable screen. Smoothness (jank) is whether scrolling and animation hold their frame budget. Memory is how much RAM the app holds — go too high and the OS kills you in the background. Battery is how much CPU, GPU, network, and GPS you burn — the silent metric users feel as a hot, draining phone. The trap is measuring on the wrong device. Your dev phone is a flagship with a fast CPU, plenty of RAM, and a warm cache. Most users are on mid- or low-tier devices with slower chips, less memory, and a flaky network. Performance work is really about the p90/p99 device and network, not the median, because the slow tail is where users churn. Two startup distinctions matter. A cold start is launching from nothing (process not in memory) — the slow, important one. A warm start resumes a backgrounded app — fast. Most of your startup effort goes into shrinking cold start: doing less before first paint, deferring everything that isn't needed for the first screen. Performance is retention. Users abandon slow-starting apps, uninstall battery hogs, and remember jank as ‘this app is broken'. App-store rankings and the OS itself reward fast apps (and kill memory-hungry ones in the background). On a low-end device, the gap between a tuned and an untuned app is the gap between ‘usable' and ‘deleted'. It's also cheaper to build in than to bolt on. Performance problems compound — a leak here, an eager init there, a chatty endpoint — until the app is sluggish everywhere and no single fix helps. Measuring early on a realistic device keeps each regression visible and cheap while it's still one isolated cause. Startup (cold vs warm): Time from tap to usable. Cold start (from nothing) is the one to optimise: do less before first paint. Jank / frame time: Dropped frames during scroll or animation. Measured per-frame against the 16ms budget — see mobile-animations. Memory & leaks: RAM held over time. Leaks (undisposed listeners/controllers, retained images) grow it until the OS kills the app. Battery & network: CPU/GPU spin, wakeups, GPS, and chatty requests. Batch work, back off polling, cache to spare the battery. Profilers: DevTools timeline, memory snapshots, the network inspector — measure first, never guess where the cost is. Profile-then-fix: Measure on a real low-end device, find the actual bottleneck, fix that one thing. The only reliable approach. Guess-and-optimise: Tune what *feels* slow without measuring. Usually optimises the wrong thing and adds complexity for no gain — the classic trap. Throw hardware at it: On the backend you can add servers; on a phone you can't. The user's device is fixed, so client perf must be earned, not bought. Native rewrite: Drop to platform-native for a hot path. Sometimes warranted; usually a last resort after profiling proves the framework isn't the cause.

chunks.title: App performance — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Do everything eagerly at startup and the app shows a white screen for three seconds on a mid-tier phone — many users never wait. Forget to dispose listeners and controllers and memory climbs until the OS silently kills the app in the background, losing the user's place. Poll an endpoint every second and the battery drains while the phone runs hot. Build a list eagerly instead of lazily and a long menu allocates thousands of off-screen rows. Each is invisible on a flagship and fatal on the device most users hold — which is exactly why you profile on the slow one. Local: it feels fast on your flagship dev phone, so you ship — and miss every problem. Production: a cold-start budget, lazy initialisation, leak-free screens, image and data caching, and testing on a real low-end device and throttled network. Enterprise: performance budgets enforced in CI (a build fails if startup or frame time regresses), a device-tier test matrix, and tracked metrics with owners. Planet-scale: real-user performance telemetry streamed from millions of devices (startup, jank, ANRs, OOM kills) broken down by device tier, OS version, and region, with automated regression alerts — you tune the slow tail of devices you'll never physically hold, guided entirely by field data.

chunks.title: App release process
chunks.text: Getting a build into millions of pockets — signing, store review, staged rollout, and fixing it fast. The app release process is everything between ‘code is done' and ‘users have it': building a signed binary, passing store review, rolling it out gradually, and shipping urgent fixes — some without a new store submission. Unlike a website you can redeploy in seconds, an app ships through gatekept stores (Apple App Store, Google Play) and lands on devices you don't control and *can't take back*. That changes everything: a bad release reaches users who may never update, so the process is built around catching problems before — and limiting blast radius after — a build goes wide. Two unavoidable gates come first. Code signing: every build is cryptographically signed with your developer certificate so the OS (and store) can prove it really came from you and wasn't tampered with — an unsigned or wrongly-signed build simply won't install. Then store review: a (partly human) check against the platform's rules, which can take hours to days and can *reject* you, so it's a step you plan around, not a formality. Once approved, you don't flip it on for everyone at once. A staged (phased) rollout releases to 1% of users, then 5, 20, 50, 100 — watching crash rates between steps, ready to halt if something spikes. And because store review is slow, two escape hatches exist: OTA (over-the-air) updates push certain code/asset changes straight to devices without a new submission, and feature flags / remote config let you turn a broken feature off instantly without shipping anything at all. The stakes are asymmetric: a web rollback is a redeploy, but a bad app build sits on millions of devices, and the users who hit the bug are often the *least* likely to update to your fix. So the process front-loads safety (beta tracks, review, signing) and builds in damage control (staged rollout, flags, OTA) precisely because ‘undo' barely exists. It also keeps releasing *boring and frequent*. Automating the build/sign/upload in CI and rolling out in stages turns shipping from a terrifying quarterly event into a routine, low-risk, halt-able process — the same philosophy as CI/CD on the backend, adapted to a world where you can't instantly take a release back. Build & versioning: A reproducible release build (in CI) with a bumped version and build number — the identity stores track updates by. Code signing: Cryptographic signature with your developer cert/key; the OS refuses to install anything signed wrong or unsigned. Store review: Apple/Google check the build against their rules; can take hours–days and can reject. Plan time for it. Staged / phased rollout: Release to a growing % of users (1→5→20→100), watching crash-free rate, with a halt button if it spikes. OTA & feature flags: Push code/asset fixes or flip features without a new submission — your fast lane around slow review. Staged rollout + crash monitoring: The standard. Release to a growing %, watch crash-free rate, halt on a spike. Safest default for native releases. Feature flags / remote config: Ship the code dark and turn it on remotely (and off instantly). Decouples ‘deployed' from ‘released' — see feature-flags. OTA / CodePush: Push approved classes of fix straight to devices, skipping review. Fast, but limited by platform rules on native code. Ship-to-everyone at once: One push, 100% immediately. Fine for a tiny user base; reckless at scale — a bad build hits everyone with no halt.

chunks.title: App release process — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Lose or leak the signing key and you can lock yourself out of ever updating the app (or let an attacker publish as you) — the worst release mistake there is. Skip the staged rollout and a crash that only shows on one OS version hits 100% of users before you notice. Ignore the crash-free metric and you ratchet a bad build wider instead of halting it. Try to OTA arbitrary native code and the store pulls your app for policy violation. Ship without feature flags and your only fix for a bad feature is another multi-day review cycle. The safe path: keys in a vault, every release staged and monitored, risky features flagged, fixes flag-flipped or OTA'd within the rules. Local: build on your laptop, sideload onto your own phone, no store involved. Production: signed builds from CI, an internal beta track, store submission, and a manual phased rollout you watch by hand with a crash reporter. Enterprise: a release-management team, automated signed pipelines, locked-down keys, feature-flag-gated launches, and dashboards tying rollout percentage to crash-free rate and business metrics. Planet-scale: continuous mobile releases on a train schedule across dozens of locales and device tiers, server-driven rollouts that auto-halt on a metric regression, OTA fast-lanes within platform rules, and crash/ANR telemetry from hundreds of millions of devices steering each rollout step automatically.

chunks.title: Deployment strategies
chunks.text: Blue-green, canary, rolling — patterns for swapping in new code without downtime or a big-bang risk. Deployment strategies are the named patterns — rolling, blue-green, canary — for replacing the running version of a service with a new one safely: no downtime, small blast radius, fast rollback. Once an app serves real traffic, ‘deploy' can't mean ‘turn it off, install the new version, turn it back on' — that's downtime, and at scale that's lost orders. Deployment strategies are the patterns for moving from version N to version N+1 *while it's running*, so users either notice nothing or, at worst, a tiny fraction hit a problem you can instantly reverse. Three classic patterns, each a different trade. Rolling: replace instances a few at a time — old and new run side by side until all are upgraded; cheap (no extra capacity) but both versions serve traffic at once. Blue-green: stand up a full second environment (green) running the new version, test it, then flip *all* traffic from the old (blue) to it at once — instant cutover and instant rollback, but you pay for two full environments. Canary: send a *small slice* of real traffic (1–5%) to the new version, watch its error and latency metrics, and only widen if it's healthy — the safest, because problems are caught on a few users, not everyone. Underneath all of them is one rule that makes safe deploys possible: the new and old versions must be able to coexist. That forces a discipline on everything they share — especially the database, where schema changes must be backward-compatible so version N keeps working while N+1 rolls out. Break that and no strategy saves you. Downtime and risk are the two things these patterns buy down. ‘Big-bang' deploys — stop everything, swap, restart — mean an outage on every release *and* an all-users blast radius if the new version is broken. Strategies turn that into either zero downtime (all of them) or a tiny, reversible exposure (canary), so releasing often stops being scary. They also make rollback a first-class, fast operation. The whole point of blue-green's warm idle environment and canary's small slice is that the answer to ‘the new version is bad' is seconds away, not a frantic redeploy. Fast, boring rollback is what lets a team deploy many times a day with confidence — the CI/CD promise, made real in production. Rolling: Upgrade instances in batches; old and new coexist during the roll. No extra capacity, but mixed versions serve traffic. Blue-green: Two full environments; test the idle one, flip all traffic at once. Instant cutover and rollback; double the cost. Canary: Route a tiny % to the new version, watch metrics, widen gradually. Smallest blast radius; needs good observability. Health checks & rollback: Automated readiness/liveness probes gate each step, and a one-command return to the last good version. Backward-compatible changes: Schema and API changes that let old and new run simultaneously — the precondition every strategy depends on. Recreate (big-bang): Stop the old, start the new. Causes downtime and an all-users blast radius; only acceptable for tiny or internal tools. Rolling: The cheap default — no extra capacity, gradual. Accepts mixed-version traffic and a slower rollback than blue-green. Blue-green: Instant cutover and instant rollback at the cost of running two full environments. Great when fast reversal matters most. Canary: Smallest blast radius and metric-gated, but needs solid observability and weighted routing to run well.

chunks.title: Deployment strategies — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Ship a breaking schema change in the same release as the code that needs it and the old, still-running version crashes the instant the migration lands — every strategy fails on a backward-incompatible change. Skip health checks and a rolling update happily replaces healthy instances with broken ones until the whole fleet is down. Canary without real metrics is just a slow big-bang — you widen a bad release blind. Run blue-green but let the database be shared and mutated incompatibly and the ‘instant rollback' rolls back code but not data. Expand-then-contract migrations, gated health checks, and metric-driven canary promotion keep every deploy zero-downtime and reversible. Local: you just restart the process — there's nobody to keep online. Production: a rolling update behind a load balancer with health checks and a one-command rollback, plus backward-compatible migrations so a redeploy never breaks the running version. Enterprise: blue-green or canary as standard, automated metric-gated promotion, and migration discipline enforced in review — deploys are routine and reversible. Planet-scale: progressive, region-by-region canary rollouts (one zone, then one region, then global), automated rollback triggered by SLO regressions, traffic shifting at the edge, and thousands of deploys a day where any single one touches only a sliver of users before it's proven safe.

chunks.title: Infrastructure as code
chunks.text: Your servers, networks, and databases defined in reviewable text files — not clicked into existence and forgotten. Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing your cloud resources — servers, databases, networks, permissions — in version-controlled files a tool applies, so infrastructure is reproducible, reviewable, and auditable instead of hand-clicked. The old way to set up infrastructure was the cloud console: a human clicks through web forms to create a server here, a database there, a firewall rule somewhere. It works once — but nobody can say exactly what exists, why, or how to recreate it, and the staging environment slowly drifts from production until ‘works in staging' means nothing. This is click-ops, and it doesn't scale. Infrastructure as code flips it: you *write down* the desired infrastructure in files — ‘two web servers of this size, one Postgres database, this network, these permissions' — and a tool reads those files and makes reality match. The files live in git alongside your app code, so infrastructure changes are reviewed in pull requests, diffed, and rolled back exactly like any other code. Most IaC tools are declarative: you describe the desired *end state*, not the steps. The tool compares that to what currently exists and computes the plan — the minimal set of creates, changes, and deletes to get there — then applies it. It keeps a record (state) of what it manages, so it knows the difference between ‘this is new' and ‘this already exists and is correct'. IaC turns infrastructure into something you can *trust and reason about*. Environments become reproducible (spin up an identical staging from the same files), changes become reviewable (a diff in a PR instead of a silent console click), and the whole setup becomes auditable (git history says who changed what, when, and why). That kills environment drift and the ‘nobody knows how prod was built' problem outright. It also makes disaster recovery and scaling real. If a region dies, you re-apply your config elsewhere and the infrastructure rebuilds itself; if you need a tenth environment for a new market, it's a parameter change, not a week of clicking. Infrastructure becomes a repeatable artifact, not a fragile hand-made one. Declarative config: Files describing the desired end state (resources, sizes, networks, permissions) — what you want, not the steps. Plan / diff: The tool previews exactly what it will create, change, or destroy before touching anything — your review gate. Apply: Executing the plan so reality matches the files; idempotent — re-running with no changes does nothing. State: The tool's record of what it manages, mapping your config to real resources so it knows what already exists. Modules / reuse: Parameterised, reusable building blocks (a ‘standard web service') so environments are consistent by construction. Click-ops (console): Click resources into being by hand. Fine for a one-off experiment; produces undocumented, drifting, irreproducible infra at any real scale. Imperative scripts: Shell/SDK scripts that issue create commands. Better than clicking, but you manage ‘already exists?' yourself and lose the plan/diff safety. Declarative IaC (Terraform/Pulumi): Describe end state; the tool computes and applies the diff. The modern default — reproducible, reviewable, idempotent. Managed PaaS config: A platform (Render/Vercel/Heroku) with a small config file (e.g. render.yaml). Less power than full IaC, far less to manage — great for small teams.

chunks.title: Infrastructure as code — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Edit a resource by hand in the console after IaC created it and you get drift — the files and reality disagree, and the next apply may ‘fix' your manual change by undoing it. Commit cloud credentials into the config files and you've leaked the keys to your whole account. Keep state on one laptop and a second engineer's apply silently clobbers your changes. Run apply without reading the plan and a careless edit destroys a production database (the diff would have screamed ‘- 1 database'). Locked remote state, secrets injected not committed, all changes through reviewed plans, and never touching managed resources by hand keep infrastructure honest. Local: no IaC — you run things on your laptop or click a free-tier resource once. Production: a single config file or Terraform project describing your real resources, in git, applied carefully (even a managed-platform render.yaml counts). Enterprise: modular IaC owned by a platform team, remote locked state, plan-on-PR and apply-on-merge through CI, with product teams composing standard modules for their services. Planet-scale: hundreds of accounts and regions described in code, policy-as-code guardrails that reject non-compliant resources at plan time, automated drift detection, and entire regions reproducible from the repository — infrastructure managed as a first-class software system in its own right.

chunks.title: Feature flags
chunks.text: Ship code dark, switch it on for whoever you choose, and kill it instantly — without a new deploy. A feature flag is a remote on/off switch wrapped around a piece of code, so you can deploy a feature turned off, enable it for a chosen slice of users, and disable it instantly — separating ‘deployed' from ‘released'. Normally, deploying code and exposing the feature are the same act — merge it, deploy it, everyone has it. A feature flag breaks that link. You wrap the new behaviour in a conditional — if (flags.newCheckout) { ...new... } else { ...old... } — and the value of that flag is controlled *remotely*, not baked into the build. So the code can ship to production off, and you turn it on later, from a dashboard, with no new deploy. That one move unlocks several things. You can roll out gradually: on for 1% of users, then 10%, then 100%, watching metrics between steps. You can target: on for internal staff, or beta testers, or one region first. You can run experiments (A/B tests): half the users see variant A, half see B, and you measure which performs better. And critically, you get a kill switch: a feature misbehaving in production is turned *off in seconds*, with no rollback, no redeploy, no waiting. Flags come in flavours. Release flags are temporary, guarding an in-progress feature until it's fully launched (then removed). Ops flags are long-lived kill switches for risky subsystems. Experiment flags drive A/B tests. Permission flags gate features to certain plans or users. They look identical in code; their *lifecycle* is what differs. Flags make releasing fundamentally safer and calmer. Decoupling deploy from release means you can merge unfinished work behind an off flag (no long-lived branches), turn features on for a few users to validate in real production, and — the big one — *kill a bad feature instantly* instead of scrambling a rollback while users suffer. The blast radius of any launch shrinks to whatever slice you chose. They also turn product decisions into measurable experiments. Instead of arguing whether the new checkout is better, you flag it on for half your users and let the conversion numbers decide. And on mobile, where you genuinely cannot redeploy fast, a flag is often the *only* fast lever you have over a feature already in users' pockets. The flag (the switch): A named condition wrapped around code; its value is read at runtime, not compiled in. Targeting rules: Who gets ‘on' — a %, a user segment, a region, internal staff — evaluated per request/user. Remote config & dashboard: Where flag values live and are changed, so flipping a flag needs no deploy. Kill switch: Flip a misbehaving feature off in seconds — incident response without a rollback. Lifecycle & cleanup: Release flags are temporary and must be removed once launched, or they rot into permanent dead branches. Deploy = release: No flags; shipping the code exposes the feature to everyone. Simplest, but every launch is all-or-nothing with no kill switch. Long-lived branches: Keep unfinished work on a branch until done. Avoids dark code in main, but causes painful merges and ‘big bang' integration. Build-time config: Bake the on/off into the build. No remote control — changing it needs a full redeploy, useless as a kill switch. Managed flag platform: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, Firebase Remote Config — targeting, dashboards, audit built in. The standard once flags get serious.

chunks.title: Feature flags — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Never clean up release flags and the codebase rots into a maze of stale if/else branches nobody dares delete — ‘flag debt' that doubles your test surface. Forget a safe default and an outage of the flag service takes your app down with it instead of failing to ‘feature off'. Use unstable targeting and a user flickers between old and new on every request. Leave a permission flag with a weak check and a user flips themselves into a paid feature. Treat flags as deliberate and temporary — stable targeting, safe defaults, server-checked permissions, and disciplined cleanup — and they stay a superpower, not a liability. Local: a boolean in a config file, flipped by hand — enough to develop a feature behind a switch. Production: a small flag service or remote config with percentage rollouts and a kill switch, values changed from a dashboard with no redeploy. Enterprise: a managed flag platform with user-segment targeting, audit logs of every flip, A/B experimentation tied to metrics, and a cleanup process that retires release flags. Planet-scale: flags evaluated in microseconds per request across millions of users with consistent bucketing, edge-evaluated for latency, integrated with experimentation pipelines and automated rollbacks, and serving as the real-time control plane for launching and killing features globally — independent of any deploy.

chunks.title: Processes & threads
chunks.text: What it actually means to 'run' a program — and how one program does several things at once. A process is a running program with its own private memory; a thread is one stream of execution inside it — and many threads let a single program do several things at the same time. When you double-click an app, the operating system creates a process: a running copy of the program, handed its own private slice of memory and its own list of open files. Two processes can't reach into each other's memory — that isolation is what stops a crashing browser tab from taking down your music player. Inside a process runs at least one thread — a single sequence of instructions being executed one after another. A thread is the thing that actually *moves* through your code, line by line. Give a process several threads and it can do several things at once: one thread redraws the screen while another waits for a file to load. The key difference: processes are isolated (separate memory, expensive to create), while threads inside one process share that process's memory (cheap to create, but they can step on each other's data — which is exactly the danger). Parallelism means truly running at the same instant on multiple CPU cores; concurrency means juggling many tasks by switching between them, even on a single core. Without multiple threads or processes, a program could only do one thing at a time: while it waited for a slow disk read, the whole app would freeze. Concurrency lets the program *stay responsive* — keep the UI alive while work happens in the background — and lets it *use all your CPU cores* instead of just one, which is the only way to go faster now that single cores have stopped getting much faster. The trade-off is difficulty. Shared memory between threads invites a whole class of subtle, intermittent bugs (race conditions) that are notoriously hard to reproduce. Processes avoid those bugs through isolation, but pay in memory and slower communication. Choosing threads vs processes is choosing between *cheap-but-dangerous sharing* and *safe-but-heavy isolation*. Process: A running program with its own private memory and resources; isolated from every other process. Thread: One stream of execution inside a process. Many threads in one process share its memory. Context switch: The OS pausing one thread and resuming another — saving and restoring its state. Fast, but not free. Scheduler: The part of the OS that decides which thread runs next, and for how long, across all CPU cores. Parallel vs concurrent: Parallel = truly at once on many cores. Concurrent = interleaved, switching fast on whatever cores exist. Event loop (async): One thread juggling thousands of waiting tasks by never blocking — Node.js's model. Great for I/O-heavy work, no shared-memory races. Multiple processes: Isolation instead of shared memory; safer, but heavier and communication is slower (you must pass messages). Coroutines / green threads: Lightweight threads the language runtime schedules itself (Go's goroutines), far cheaper than OS threads.

chunks.title: Processes & threads — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Spawn a thread for every one of 50,000 incoming connections and the machine thrashes: each thread costs memory and the scheduler spends more time context-switching than doing work. Or let two threads update the same balance without coordination and the number comes out wrong only sometimes — a bug that vanishes the moment you try to reproduce it. The fixes: bound your threads (a pool, or an event loop), and guard shared data. On a tiny script, one thread is plenty. A busy server uses a pool of threads or an event loop to serve thousands of connections on a handful of cores. At planet scale you spread across many machines (many processes on many hosts), and the hard coordination problem moves from 'threads sharing memory' up to 'machines sharing a network' — the world of distributed systems.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Memory: the stack & the heap
chunks.title: Memory: the stack & the heap
chunks.text: Where your variables actually live while a program runs — and why some memory cleans itself up and some doesn't. Running programs keep data in two main places: the stack (fast, automatic, for short-lived local variables) and the heap (flexible, manual-ish, for data that must outlive the function that made it). While a program runs, its variables have to live *somewhere* in the computer's memory (RAM). There are two main regions, and they behave very differently. The stack is a neat pile that grows and shrinks automatically as functions are called and return. The heap is a big open space where you ask for memory on demand and it stays until it's freed. The stack holds the local variables of whatever function is running right now. Call a function and a new stack frame is pushed on top, holding its locals; when the function returns, that frame is popped and its memory is instantly reclaimed. It's blazing fast and fully automatic — but everything on it disappears the moment the function ends, and it's small. The heap is for data that must *outlive* the function that created it, or that's too big or whose size isn't known in advance — a list that grows, an image you loaded, an object you'll hand to another part of the program. You allocate it explicitly (or the language does), and it lives until someone frees it. The catch: somebody has to remember to free it, or it leaks. You need both because programs have two kinds of data. Short-lived scratch values (a loop counter, a sum) want the stack's speed and automatic cleanup. Data that must survive past one function, or whose size you can't know upfront, *needs* the heap — there's no other place to put it. Using one region for everything would be either far too slow (heap-only) or impossible (stack-only can't hold growing or long-lived data). The trade-off is who carries the burden of cleanup. Manual heap management (C) is fast and predictable but error-prone — leaks and corruption are some of the nastiest bugs in software. Automatic management (garbage collection) removes those bugs but adds occasional pauses and overhead. This single choice shapes the feel of a whole language. Stack: Fast, automatic memory for a function's local variables. Grows on call, shrinks on return. Small and short-lived. Stack frame: The block pushed for one function call, holding its locals and where to return to. Popped when it returns. Heap: Flexible memory you request on demand for longer-lived or larger data. Stays until freed. Pointer / reference: A small value on the stack that holds the *address* of something in the heap — the warehouse ticket. Garbage collector: In many languages, an automatic janitor that finds heap data nobody references anymore and frees it. Garbage collection: An automatic janitor frees unreferenced heap memory (Java, Python, JS, Dart). Safe and easy; costs some pauses and memory. Manual management: You allocate and free by hand (C, C++). Maximum control and speed; leaks and double-frees are on you. Ownership / borrow checker: The compiler proves when to free (Rust). No GC, no leaks — at the cost of a stricter language to satisfy.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Memory: the stack & the heap
chunks.title: Memory: the stack & the heap — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Recurse too deep and you blow the stack — a stack overflow crash, because the pile of frames hit its small limit. On the heap, forget to free (or hold a reference you don't need) and memory creeps up until the program is killed — a leak. Free something twice, or use a pointer after freeing it, and you corrupt memory in ways that crash much later, far from the real bug. Knowing which region a value lives in is the first step to diagnosing all of these. On a small program none of this is visible. In a long-running server, a slow heap leak that's invisible for an hour becomes an out-of-memory crash overnight — which is why production servers watch memory as closely as CPU. At massive scale, garbage-collection pauses become a latency problem teams tune for years, and the choice of a non-GC language (Rust, C++) for the hottest paths is often about exactly this.

chunks.title: Locks, mutexes & semaphores
chunks.text: The tools that let many threads touch shared data without corrupting it — and the new bug they introduce. Locks, mutexes, and semaphores are the basic tools for coordinating threads so only the allowed number touch shared data at a time — turning chaotic collisions into orderly turns. When several threads share memory, two of them changing the same data at the same instant produces a race condition — a wrong result that appears only sometimes, depending on exact timing. Concurrency primitives are the small set of tools that prevent this by controlling *who* may touch shared data, and *how many* at once. A mutex (short for *mutual exclusion*) is the workhorse: a lock that exactly one thread can hold at a time. A thread *acquires* the mutex before touching the shared data and *releases* it after; any other thread that tries to acquire it must wait its turn. The protected stretch of code is called the critical section — the part only one thread may be inside at once. A semaphore is a counter that allows up to *N* threads through at once (a mutex is just a semaphore with N=1). Use it to say 'at most 5 threads may use the database connection pool simultaneously'. Other tools — condition variables (wait until something becomes true) and atomic operations (a single uninterruptible read-modify-write) — round out the toolbox for finer or faster coordination. Without coordination, shared-memory concurrency is simply incorrect: the classic 'two requests both spend the same points' bug conjures value out of thin air. Primitives are the difference between a balance you can trust and one that goes wrong under load. They're the price of admission for letting threads share memory at all. But they introduce a brand-new failure mode: deadlock. If thread A holds lock 1 and waits for lock 2, while thread B holds lock 2 and waits for lock 1, both wait forever and the program freezes. There's also contention — if everything fights over one lock, threads spend their time waiting instead of working, and adding more cores stops helping. So the trade-off is: locks buy correctness, but careless locking buys deadlocks and lost performance. Mutex / lock: Only one thread may hold it at a time. Acquire before the shared data, release after. The default tool. Critical section: The stretch of code a mutex protects — the part only one thread may execute at once. Semaphore: A counter permitting up to N threads through at once. Caps how many use a limited resource. Condition variable: Lets a thread sleep until another signals 'the thing you waited for is true now' — no busy-waiting. Atomic operation: A single read-modify-write the CPU guarantees can't be interrupted — a lock-free way to bump a counter. Atomic operations: For single-variable updates, a lock-free CPU instruction is correct and faster — no waiting at all. Message passing: Don't share memory; have threads send each other messages (Go channels, the actor model). Sidesteps locks entirely. Immutable data: If shared data never changes, no coordination is needed — only writes need protecting. Push it to the database: Let the database serialize the conflicting write (a conditional update), instead of locking in your app.

chunks.title: Locks, mutexes & semaphores — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Forget to release a lock (an early return, an exception) and every other thread waits forever — the app hangs with no crash to point at. Acquire two locks in different orders in different threads and you deadlock. Lock too coarsely and your 8-core machine runs like a 1-core one because everyone queues on the same lock. The cures: always release (use language features that guarantee it), impose a global lock-ordering, and keep critical sections tiny. On one machine, mutexes and atomics are the whole story. The instant your data lives across *several* machines, an in-process lock is useless — there's no shared memory to guard — and you need a distributed lock (via Redis or a consensus system) or, better, a design that avoids shared mutable state. The coordination problem doesn't disappear as you scale; it gets harder, which is why distributed systems lean toward immutability and message passing.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — What an operating system does
chunks.title: What an operating system does
chunks.text: The invisible manager between your code and the bare hardware — sharing one machine safely among many programs. An operating system is the master program that shares the CPU, memory, and devices among all your other programs, keeps them isolated from each other, and gives them a clean way to ask the hardware for things. Your computer's hardware — the CPU, the RAM, the disk, the network card — is dumb and shared. Something has to decide which program gets the CPU right now, hand each program its own memory, and stop one program from scribbling over another's data or seizing the whole machine. That something is the operating system (OS) — Windows, macOS, Linux, Android. The heart of the OS is the kernel: the always-resident core that has full, privileged control of the hardware. Everything else — your apps, your browser — runs as ordinary, *unprivileged* programs that must politely *ask* the kernel whenever they want to touch hardware. That request is called a system call (a 'syscall'): 'read this file', 'send these bytes', 'give me more memory'. The OS does four big jobs: it schedules the CPU among all running threads (so each gets a fair turn), manages memory (giving each process its own private address space), manages devices through drivers (translating 'save this file' into the exact signals a particular disk understands), and enforces isolation and permissions (so your photo app can't read your banking app's memory or your private files). Without an OS, every program would have to talk to every model of disk and network card directly, would have to manually avoid every other program's memory, and any single bug could freeze or corrupt the whole machine. The OS exists to make hardware *shareable* and *safe*: it abstracts a thousand kinds of hardware behind one clean interface, and it enforces the boundaries that let mutually-distrusting programs coexist on one chip. The trade-off is a layer of overhead and indirection. Every system call costs a little time crossing into the kernel; virtual memory adds a translation step. For 99.9% of software that's a bargain. For the most extreme performance work (high-frequency trading, some databases) people fight to *avoid* the kernel on hot paths — proof of how much the OS is normally doing for you. Scheduler: Decides which thread runs on each CPU core and for how long, switching fast to keep everything responsive. Memory manager: Gives each process a private address space and maps it to real RAM — with the illusion of more memory than exists. System calls: The guarded doorway programs use to ask the kernel for hardware actions: read, write, network, allocate. Drivers: Per-device translators that turn generic requests into the exact commands a specific piece of hardware needs. User vs kernel mode: Apps run restricted (user mode); the kernel runs privileged (kernel mode). Crossing over is a system call. Bare-metal / no OS: Embedded chips and tiny devices run one program directly on hardware — maximal control, none of the safety or sharing. Real-time OS (RTOS): A specialized OS that guarantees response within strict time bounds — for cars, medical devices, robots. Hypervisor / VM: A layer below the OS that runs *several* whole operating systems on one machine — the basis of cloud servers. Unikernel: Bundle just your app with a minimal kernel into one image — tiny and fast, less general-purpose.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — What an operating system does
chunks.title: What an operating system does — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Open more files than the OS's limit and your server starts refusing connections with a cryptic 'too many open files'. Use more memory than RAM and the OS pages to disk — the machine grinds to a crawl (thrashing) or the kernel's out-of-memory killer abruptly kills your process. A buggy driver, running in privileged kernel mode, can crash the entire system (the 'blue screen'). Most production server tuning is really about respecting the OS's limits. On one laptop the OS quietly juggles your apps. On a server it's tuned hard — raising file-descriptor limits, sizing memory, pinning processes to cores. In the cloud, a hypervisor slices one physical machine into many virtual ones, each with its own OS, and containers pack many isolated apps onto one OS kernel. At planet scale, custom kernels and kernel-bypass networking squeeze out the last microseconds — the OS is still there, just sculpted for the workload.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — How the internet works
chunks.title: How the internet works
chunks.text: The journey of your data — chopped into packets, addressed, and hopped across the planet to a specific machine. The internet moves data by chopping it into small labelled packets, each stamped with a destination IP address, then hopping them router-to-router across many independent networks until they reach the right machine. The internet is not one wire — it's a vast mesh of independent networks (your home, your ISP, data centers, undersea cables) that agree to pass data to each other. When you load a page, your data doesn't travel as one big stream; it's chopped into small chunks called packets, and each packet finds its own way across the mesh. Every device on the internet has an IP address — a numeric label like 142.250.72.14 — that uniquely identifies it, the way a postal address identifies a house. Each packet is stamped with the destination IP. Specialized computers called routers sit at the junctions between networks; a router reads a packet's destination and forwards it one hop closer, handing it to the next router, and so on, until it arrives. This is organized in layers, each handling one concern and not caring how the others work. Roughly: the link layer moves bits over one physical link (Wi-Fi, ethernet); IP addresses and routes packets across networks; TCP/UDP turn packets into a usable conversation between two programs; and the application layer (HTTP, email) is the actual message. Each layer wraps the one above it in its own envelope — like nesting letters in envelopes inside envelopes. The internet was designed to survive failure. Packet-switching (chopping data into independently-routed packets) means there's no single fixed circuit to break: if a cable is cut or a router dies, packets simply reroute around it. Compare the old telephone network, which reserved one dedicated circuit per call — efficient for a steady voice stream, but a single break dropped the call, and idle circuits wasted capacity. Packets share every link dynamically and heal around damage. The trade-off is that 'best-effort' delivery makes no guarantees — packets can be lost, duplicated, delayed, or reordered. That unreliability is intentional: it keeps the network core dumb, cheap, and fast, and lets the *endpoints* add exactly the guarantees they need (reliability via TCP, or raw speed via UDP). This 'smart edges, dumb core' principle is why the internet scaled to billions of devices. Packet: A small chunk of your data wrapped with addressing labels. The unit the internet actually moves. IP address: The numeric address of a machine (IPv4 like 142.x.x.x, or the newer, vast IPv6). Where a packet is headed. Router: A junction computer that reads a packet's destination and forwards it one hop closer along the best path it knows. Link layer: Moves bits across one physical hop — your Wi-Fi, an ethernet cable, a fiber line — between two directly-connected devices. Layered model (TCP/IP): Link → Internet (IP) → Transport (TCP/UDP) → Application (HTTP). Each layer wraps the one above and ignores the rest. Circuit switching: Reserve a dedicated path end-to-end (old phone networks). Steady and ordered, but wasteful and fragile to any break. IPv6 vs IPv4: IPv4's ~4 billion addresses ran out; IPv6 offers a practically unlimited supply. Both route packets the same way. Private networks / VPNs: Run an addressed, routed network within or across the internet, tunneled and often encrypted.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — How the internet works
chunks.title: How the internet works — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: A misbehaving router announcing wrong routes (a BGP leak) can silently black-hole traffic for whole regions — this has knocked major sites offline globally. Closer to home, running out of IPv4 addresses forced the patchwork of NAT (sharing one public address among many devices), which complicates direct connections. And because the core only promises best-effort, congestion shows up as packet loss and lag, which the upper layers must absorb. From two laptops on the same Wi-Fi to billions of devices worldwide, the *same* packet-and-IP model holds — that's the triumph of the design. Scale shows up as more routers, bigger backbone links, undersea cables, and content pushed physically closer to users (CDNs) so packets travel fewer hops. The addressing had to scale too: IPv4's exhaustion drove the move to IPv6's effectively limitless space.

chunks.title: TCP vs UDP
chunks.text: Two ways to send data over the internet: reliable-but-careful, or fast-but-careless — and when each is right.
